title: Water and salt: how humans, fish and desert animals keep the balance

summary.text: A sea fish swims in water all day, yet she must keep drinking so that she does not dry out. A river fish hardly ever drinks. Why are they so different? In this lesson you will pull water out of cucumber slices using only salt, find out why sea water cannot quench thirst, and see how kidneys, gills and the white cap on a gecko's dropping all deal with the same two problems.
summary.art: A mackerel in blue sea water with her mouth open, drinking, beside a rohu in green river water with her mouth shut, and a small bowl of salted cucumber slices sitting in a pool of water between them.

intro.hook: A sailor's boat has run out of drinking water. The sea is all around her, as far as she can see. Should she drink the sea water? Say yes or no, and say why you think so.
intro.text: Almost everyone answers no. Very few people can say the reason. Sea water is water, after all, and the sailor's body is short of water. First you will taste three waters. Then you will run a test with cucumber and salt, and the result will give you the reason. By the end you will be able to answer for the sailor. You will also be able to answer for a hilsa swimming from the sea into a river, and for a camel walking across the Thar.
intro.art: A woman alone in a small fishing boat on a wide flat sea, holding an empty steel water bottle upside down and looking at the water around her.

outcomes: I can explain osmosis: which way water moves across a cell's membrane, and why.
I can explain why drinking sea water leaves a person with less water than before.
I can explain how my kidneys make urine stronger or weaker, and what the water-saving hormone does.
I can name the three nitrogen wastes, say which animals make each one, and say why.
I can explain the opposite water problems of a river fish and a sea fish, and how each fish solves hers.
I can name four ways a desert animal saves water.
I can run a fair test with cucumber and salt, and say what my results show.
I can explain why a rehydration drink needs both salt and sugar.

terms.meaning: A solid dissolves when it breaks up into particles too small to see and spreads all through a liquid.
terms.example: Salt stirred into rasam dissolves. You cannot see it any more, but you can taste it in every spoonful.
terms.art: A spoon of salt being stirred into a steel tumbler of water, with the grains fading as they sink.

terms.meaning: Concentration is how much of something is dissolved in a set amount of liquid. A strong, or concentrated, liquid has a lot dissolved in it. A weak, or dilute, liquid has only a little.
terms.example: Sea water has about 35 grams of salt in each litre. That is nearly four times the concentration of salt in your blood.
terms.art: Two tumblers of water side by side, one with a few dots of salt drawn inside it and one crowded with dots.

terms.meaning: A cell membrane is the very thin skin around every living cell. Water passes through it easily. Salt and sugar pass only through special doors in it.
terms.example: Each cell in a cucumber slice is wrapped in a membrane. Water leaves through it when you put salt outside.
terms.art: A zoomed-in drawing of one rounded cell with a thin double-line skin, and small water drops passing through the skin in both directions.

terms.meaning: Osmosis is the movement of water through a membrane, from the side with less dissolved in it to the side with more dissolved in it.
terms.example: Dry raisins dropped into water swell up in a few hours. Water moves by osmosis into the sugary inside of each raisin.
terms.art: A wrinkled raisin and a plump raisin, with arrows showing water going into the plump one.

terms.meaning: Osmoregulation is the work a living body does to keep the water and salt inside it at steady levels.
terms.example: After a salty meal of pickle and rice, you feel thirsty and pass less urine. Both are part of your osmoregulation.
terms.art: A child drinking a tumbler of water after a meal, with a small drawing of two kidneys beside her.

terms.meaning: A pump is a protein in a cell membrane that uses energy to carry one kind of particle across, even towards the side that already has more of it.
terms.example: Pumps in the wall of a kidney tube push salt out of the urine and into the kidney around it.
terms.art: A section of cell membrane with a small gate-shaped protein carrying a salt particle across, and a lightning mark to show energy.

terms.meaning: An aquaporin is a water door: a protein in a cell membrane with a hole so narrow that only water can pass through it.
terms.example: Your kidney cells add more aquaporins to their membranes when your body needs to save water.
terms.art: A cell membrane with a tube-shaped protein through it and a single file of water particles passing down the tube.

terms.meaning: Nitrogen waste is the waste left over when cells break down protein. Protein contains nitrogen, and the body cannot store the extra.
terms.example: After you eat dal, paneer, egg or fish, your cells use the protein. The nitrogen they do not need leaves in your urine as urea.
terms.art: A plate of dal and rice with an arrow to a body outline, and a second arrow from the kidneys labelled nitrogen waste.

terms.meaning: Ammonia is the first nitrogen waste every animal cell makes. It is poisonous, and it dissolves very easily in water.
terms.example: A rohu in a pond lets ammonia pass out through her gills, straight into the water around her.
terms.art: A carp-like fish in a pond with small dots leaving her gill cover and spreading into the water.

terms.meaning: Urea is a nitrogen waste that the liver makes out of ammonia. It is far less poisonous than ammonia, so the body can carry it in the blood until the kidneys remove it.
terms.example: Humans, cows, dogs and adult frogs all send out most of their nitrogen waste as urea in urine.
terms.art: A body outline with an arrow from the liver to the kidneys, labelled urea.

terms.meaning: Uric acid is a nitrogen waste that hardly dissolves in water. An animal can send it out as a white paste, using very little water.
terms.example: The white cap on a house gecko's dropping is nitrogen waste made from uric acid.
terms.art: A small dark gecko dropping with a white tip, on a wall near a tube light.

terms.meaning: The loop of Henle is the hairpin-shaped part of each tiny kidney tube. It makes the deep part of the kidney very salty.
terms.example: A kangaroo rat has very long loops of Henle for the size of her kidneys. She can make urine nearly five times as strong as the strongest human urine.
terms.art: One kidney tube drawn as a long hairpin dipping down into a darker, saltier zone of the kidney and coming back up.

terms.meaning: A collecting duct is the last tube that urine passes through in the kidney. Here the kidney decides how much water to take back.
terms.example: On a hot day when you have drunk little, your collecting ducts let a lot of water go back into the blood. Your urine comes out dark and strong.
terms.art: A straight tube running down through a salty zone of the kidney, with water drops leaving the tube sideways.

terms.meaning: ADH is a chemical message made in the brain. It tells the collecting ducts in the kidneys to let more water go back into the blood. ADH is short for antidiuretic hormone.
terms.example: When your blood becomes a little too salty, your brain releases more ADH within minutes.
terms.art: A side view of a head with a small gland under the brain, and a dotted arrow running down through the blood to the two kidneys.

terms.meaning: Gills are the thin, feathery organs with which a fish takes oxygen from water. Their surface is very thin, so water and salt also cross it.
terms.example: Lift the gill cover of a fresh mackerel at the fish market. The dark red, comb-like gills are underneath.
terms.art: A fish with her gill cover lifted to show rows of red comb-like gills.

terms.meaning: A salt gland is an organ that pumps extra salt out of the blood as a very salty liquid. Seabirds, sea turtles and some other sea animals have salt glands.
terms.example: A sea turtle on a beach seems to be crying. The thick tears are salt leaving through the salt glands beside her eyes.
terms.art: The head of an olive ridley sea turtle on a sandy beach at night with a thick clear tear running from the corner of her eye.

terms.meaning: Metabolic water is new water that cells make when they use food for energy. The hydrogen in the food joins with oxygen from the air and forms water.
terms.example: A kangaroo rat makes about 54 grams of water inside her body from every 100 grams of dry barley she eats.
terms.art: A small desert rodent holding a seed, with a drop of water drawn inside her body outline.

terms.meaning: A contractile vacuole is a tiny bag inside a one-celled pond creature. It fills with the water that keeps coming in, then squeezes the water out.
terms.example: A Paramecium in pond water empties their contractile vacuoles every few seconds, all day and all night.
terms.art: A slipper-shaped one-celled creature with a star-shaped bag inside, squirting a drop of water out through the cell's edge.

terms.meaning: Brackish water is water that is saltier than a river but less salty than the sea. It is found where a river meets the sea.
terms.example: The backwaters of Kerala and the water among the mangroves at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu are brackish.
terms.art: A river mouth seen from above, with green river water mixing into blue sea water and mangrove trees along the bank.

terms.meaning: Dehydration is the state of a body that has lost more water than it has taken in.
terms.example: After a long day of cricket in May with nothing to drink, you have a dry mouth, a headache and very dark urine. These are signs of dehydration.
terms.art: A tired child sitting in the shade of a neem tree with a cricket bat, reaching for a water bottle.

terms.meaning: ORS is a drink of clean water with measured amounts of salt and sugar. It replaces the water and salt a person loses in diarrhoea. ORS is short for oral rehydration solution.
terms.example: A health worker gives a packet of ORS to mix in one litre of water for a child with loose motions.
terms.art: A packet of ORS powder being poured into a one-litre steel jug of water, with a spoon ready to stir.

explanations.concept: A body has two jobs to do with water
explanations.definition: Excretion is sending out the wastes that the body's cells have made. Osmoregulation is keeping the water and salt in the body at steady levels.
explanations.description: Your kidneys filter your blood and take back what the body needs. What is left leaves as urine. That is the kidney's first job, removing waste. The kidneys have a second job that matters just as much. They keep your blood at almost exactly the same saltiness all the time. Your blood is about as salty as water with 9 grams of salt in each litre. Why must it stay there? Every cell in your body sits in liquid that comes from the blood. If that liquid turns too salty, water leaves the cells and they shrink. If it turns too watery, water enters the cells and they swell. Brain cells are packed inside the skull with no room to swell, so even a small change can make a person confused and ill. Every animal has to do both jobs. A fish, a camel and a gecko each do them in a different way, because each has a different amount of water to spare.
examples: After a salty meal you feel thirsty and pass less urine. Your body is bringing its saltiness back down.
After two tumblers of water you pass a lot of pale urine within the hour. Your body is sending the extra water out.
A camel, a hilsa and a house gecko all have to remove nitrogen waste. Each uses a different amount of water to do it.
explanations.art: A child's body outline with the two kidneys coloured in, and two labels beside them: remove the waste, and keep water and salt steady.

explanations.concept: Osmosis: water moves towards the side with more dissolved in it
explanations.definition: Osmosis is the movement of water through a membrane, from the side with less dissolved in it to the side with more dissolved in it.
explanations.description: Every cell is wrapped in a membrane. Water passes through it easily, but dissolved salt mostly does not. Now put plain water on one side and salty water on the other. Water particles are always moving, and they cross the membrane in both directions. On the salty side, each salt particle holds a small crowd of water particles around it. Those water particles are less free to cross. So more water crosses from the plain side to the salty side than comes back. The salty side gains water, and nobody has pushed anything. This is a simplified picture. The full account uses a measure of how free the water particles are to move, which scientists call water potential. The rule you can rely on is simple: water moves towards the side with more dissolved in it. It does not have to be salt. Sugar, urea or anything else that cannot cross the membrane has the same effect.
examples: Salt sprinkled on cucumber slices makes a very salty film on the cut faces. Water leaves the cells and collects in the bowl.
Raisins soaked in water swell up, because the inside of a raisin is full of sugar.
Salt keeps lime pickle and dried fish from rotting. It draws water out of the cells of microbes by osmosis, so the microbes cannot grow.
explanations.art: A box divided by a dotted membrane, with plain water on the left and water crowded with salt dots on the right, and a thick arrow of water going from left to right.

explanations.concept: No cell pumps water: a body moves salt, and the water follows
explanations.definition: Animal cells have pumps for salt, but no pump for water has been found. To move water, a body moves salt first. Then water follows by osmosis.
explanations.description: A pump is a protein in a cell membrane that uses energy to carry a particle across. In 1957 the Danish scientist Jens Christian Skou found the pump that carries sodium, which is one half of salt. Your cells spend a large share of their energy running these sodium pumps. For water, cells have only doors. Water can also seep slowly through the membrane itself, and the doors make the crossing much faster. In 1992 Peter Agre and his team in the United States found the first water door, and it was named an aquaporin. A door lets water through in either direction, and osmosis decides which way it goes. So when a kidney tube needs to take water back from the urine, it pumps salt out of the tube. The space outside the tube becomes saltier, and water follows through the aquaporins. Your gut takes in water the same way after a drink. Sweat glands, tear glands and a fish's gills all work like this too. A few scientists think that some salt carriers drag a little water through with them. That is still being argued about. Either way, water moves only because something else was moved first.
examples: In the gut, cells pump salt from the food side to the blood side. The water you drank follows it.
In a kidney tube, salt is pumped out and water follows it back to the blood.
In a sweat gland, salt is moved into the tube of the gland first. Water follows it, and that water is your sweat.
explanations.art: A cell membrane with a pump protein pushing salt particles across, and beside it an open water door with water particles drifting through after the salt.

explanations.concept: How a kidney makes urine stronger than blood
explanations.definition: The loop of Henle is a hairpin-shaped part of each kidney tube. It makes the deep part of the kidney very salty, so that water can be drawn out of the urine there.
explanations.description: To save water, a kidney must make urine that is stronger than blood. That means taking water out of the urine. But no cell can pump water. So the kidney builds a very salty zone deep inside itself, and lets osmosis do the work. Each kidney tube has a long loop shaped like a hairpin. It dips down into the deep part of the kidney and comes back up. The wall of the upward half pumps salt out into the kidney around it, and it has no water doors, so the water cannot follow. Salt builds up around the loop. Because the two halves of the hairpin lie side by side with liquid flowing in opposite directions, the effect is multiplied along the length of the loop. The deepest part of a human kidney becomes about four times as concentrated as blood. Part of that is urea, which the kidney also collects there. We call it the salty zone to keep things simple. Last of all, the urine runs down through this salty zone inside a collecting duct. If the wall of the duct has its water doors open, water leaves the urine by osmosis and goes back to the blood. What is left is strong urine. In 1951 Heinrich Wirz, Bartholomew Hargitay and Werner Kuhn in Basel showed that the salty zone is real. They froze thin slices of rat kidney and measured them from the outside of the kidney to its deepest tip. The slices grew steadily more concentrated towards the tip.
examples: The strongest human urine is about four times as concentrated as blood.
A kangaroo rat's loops of Henle are very long for the size of her kidney. Her urine can be nearly five times as strong as the strongest human urine.
A beaver lives in fresh water and has short loops. A beaver's strongest urine is weaker than a human's.
explanations.art: A cross-section of a kidney shaded from pale at the outside to dark at the centre, with one hairpin loop dipping into the dark zone and a straight collecting duct beside it.

explanations.concept: The water-saving hormone sets how much water goes back
explanations.definition: ADH is a hormone, which means a chemical message carried in the blood. It tells the collecting ducts of the kidneys to open more water doors, so that more water returns to the blood.
explanations.description: A small part of your brain called the hypothalamus has cells that respond to how salty the blood is. When you sweat a lot or drink too little, your blood becomes slightly saltier. These cells shrink a little, and they signal the pituitary gland just below the brain. The pituitary releases ADH into the blood. Within minutes the ADH reaches the kidneys. The cells of the collecting ducts then move more aquaporins into their membranes. More water leaves the urine and returns to the blood, and you pass a small amount of dark urine. The same brain cells make you feel thirsty. When you drink a lot, the opposite happens. The blood becomes slightly more watery, less ADH is released, and the cells take their water doors back inside. Water stays in the urine, and you pass a lot of pale urine. In this way an adult's kidneys can make as little as about half a litre of urine in a day, or many litres. They cannot make none at all. The day's urea and other wastes need some water to carry them out.
examples: On a hot afternoon of play with little to drink, your urine is dark yellow and there is not much of it. Your ADH is high.
After two tumblers of water on a cool day, your urine is pale and plentiful. Your ADH is low.
Urine is usually darker first thing in the morning. ADH stays high during sleep, when you are not drinking.
explanations.art: A side view of a head showing a small region low in the brain and a pea-sized gland under it, with a dotted arrow through the bloodstream to a kidney whose collecting duct has small doors opening.

explanations.concept: Why sea water cannot quench thirst
explanations.definition: Sea water has more salt in it than the strongest urine a human kidney can make. To send out the salt from sea water, the body must use more water than the sea water brought in.
explanations.description: Sea water has about 35 grams of salt in each litre. Your blood is about as salty as 9 grams in a litre. Suppose the sailor drinks one litre of sea water. Her gut takes in the salt, and the water follows it into the blood. Now her blood has 35 grams of extra salt, and her kidneys must send it out. Human urine at its strongest can hold only about 20 grams of salt in a litre. Much of the kidney's concentrating power is used up by urea and the other wastes that must also leave. So 35 grams of salt needs about one and three quarter litres of urine. She drank one litre and must pass one and three quarter litres. She ends up with about three quarters of a litre less water than before she drank. Sea water also contains magnesium and sulphate. The gut takes these in poorly, so they stay in the gut and hold water there. That can cause loose motions, which lose still more water. So the sailor should not drink. She should catch rain, and keep out of the sun.
examples: The English poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge wrote in 1798 about sailors stuck on a still sea: 'Water, water, every where, nor any drop to drink.'
A kangaroo rat's kidneys can make urine much stronger than sea water. A human's kidneys cannot make urine that holds as much salt as sea water does.
Ships and coastal cities make fresh water from sea water with machines. Chennai has large plants that do this.
explanations.art: Three measuring jugs in a row: one litre of sea water going in, a jug labelled 35 grams of salt, and a larger jug of one and three quarter litres of urine coming out.

explanations.concept: Three nitrogen wastes: ammonia, urea and uric acid
explanations.definition: Nitrogen waste is what is left when cells break down protein. Animals send it out as ammonia, as urea or as uric acid, depending on how much water they can spare.
explanations.description: Starch, oil and sugar are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. When cells use them for energy, they turn into carbon dioxide and water. Protein is the body-building part of food, found in dal, milk, eggs, fish and meat. Protein also contains nitrogen. When cells break down protein they do not need, the nitrogen comes off as ammonia. Ammonia is poisonous, so it cannot be allowed to build up. It dissolves very easily, so an animal who lives in water can let it wash away. Most fish and tadpoles do this. Their ammonia passes out through the gills, and it costs them almost no energy. An animal on land cannot spare that much water. So the liver joins ammonia with carbon dioxide and makes urea. Making urea costs energy. But urea is much less poisonous, so it can travel in the blood, and it needs roughly a tenth of the water. Mammals, adult frogs and sharks make urea. Birds, lizards, snakes and insects go one step further and make uric acid. It costs even more energy. But it hardly dissolves, so it can leave the body as a paste with very little water. A tadpole makes ammonia, and the same animal as a grown frog on land makes urea. In 1931 the biochemist Joseph Needham gave a reason why birds and reptiles use uric acid. Their young grow inside a shelled egg, where waste cannot be washed away. Solid grains of uric acid can sit in the egg without harming the chick. Most biologists still find this likely.
examples: Fish and tadpoles: ammonia, washed away through the gills.
Humans, cows, dogs and adult frogs: urea, dissolved in urine.
Crows, pigeons, geckos, snakes and cockroaches: a paste made from uric acid. It is the white part of a bird's or a gecko's dropping.
Humans also make a little uric acid, from worn-out DNA. If too much builds up, it can form sharp crystals in a joint. That illness is called gout.
explanations.art: Three animals in a row with what each sends out: a fish with dots leaving her gills, a girl with a drop of urine, and a crow with a white-and-dark dropping.

explanations.concept: A river fish has too much water coming in
explanations.definition: A river fish is saltier inside than the water around her. Water enters her body by osmosis all the time, and she must keep sending it out.
explanations.description: The blood of a bony fish is about one third as salty as the sea. River and pond water has almost no salt. So for a rohu or a catla in a pond, the inside is far saltier than the outside. Her gills must be thin, so that oxygen can cross them. Water crosses them too. It moves in by osmosis all day, and a little of her salt leaks out. If she did nothing, she would swell and her blood would become too watery. So she does three things. She hardly drinks at all. Her kidneys make a large amount of very weak urine, which sends the water out and keeps most of the salt in. And special cells in her gills pump salt in from the water, even though the water holds very little. The Danish scientist August Krogh showed in the 1930s that freshwater fish and frogs can take up salt from very dilute water in this way.
examples: A rohu, a catla and a murrel in a village tank all have this problem.
A goldfish in a bowl passes a lot of very dilute urine all day.
A frog sitting in a pond takes in water through her skin, and does not need to drink with her mouth.
explanations.art: A rohu in green pond water with thin blue arrows of water entering at her gills, a large pale stream of urine leaving, and tiny salt dots being pulled in at the gills.

explanations.concept: A sea fish has water leaking out all day
explanations.definition: A bony sea fish is less salty inside than the sea around her. Water leaves her body by osmosis all the time, so she must drink sea water and send the salt out.
explanations.description: A mackerel, a sardine or a pomfret has blood about one third as salty as the sea. So the outside is saltier than the inside. Water leaves through her thin gills by osmosis, all day. She lives in water and is always in danger of drying out. Her answer is to drink the sea. In 1930 the American scientist Homer Smith showed that bony sea fish swallow sea water steadily. In the gut, cells pump the salt into the blood, and the water follows it. Now she has the water, and far too much salt. Her kidneys cannot make urine saltier than her blood. So special cells in her gills pump the salt straight out into the sea. Ancel Keys and Edward Willmer described these cells in the gills of eels in 1932. Her kidneys make only a little urine, which carries out magnesium and sulphate. All this pumping costs energy. That is the reason a sea fish and a river fish cannot simply swap places. Each one's gills are set to pump salt in one direction only.
examples: Mackerel, sardines, seer fish and pomfret all drink sea water and pump the salt out at their gills.
A sea fish put into fresh water takes in water and swells. Her gills are still pumping salt out when she needs it pumped in.
A river fish put into sea water loses water and shrivels. Her gills are still pumping salt in.
explanations.art: A mackerel in blue sea water with her mouth open swallowing water, blue arrows of water leaving at her gills, and salt dots being pushed out from the gills.

explanations.concept: Sharks, hilsa and the fish who change waters
explanations.definition: Sharks keep urea in their blood so that they are as concentrated as the sea. Some fish, such as hilsa, can reverse the salt pumps in their gills and move between sea and river.
explanations.description: Sharks and rays solved the sea's problem in another way. They do not send out all their urea. They keep so much of it in the blood that their body is as concentrated as sea water, or slightly more. So water does not leave them by osmosis, and they do not need to drink. The extra salt from their food leaves through a salt gland near the end of the gut, called the rectal gland. When shark or ray meat is kept too long, bacteria turn the urea into ammonia. That is the sharp smell of stale shark. A few fish live in both waters. The hilsa, called ilish in Bengali and pulasa in Telugu, grows up in the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. In the monsoon she swims up rivers such as the Hooghly, the Godavari and the Narmada to lay her eggs. On the way she passes through an estuary, where the river meets the sea and the water is brackish. There her body changes over. Her gill cells stop pumping salt out and begin to pump it in. She stops drinking, and her kidneys begin to make plenty of weak urine. Salmon make the same change, and eels make it in the other direction.
examples: Hilsa enter the Godavari when the monsoon floods come down, mainly from July to September.
Pearl spot, called karimeen in Kerala, live in the brackish backwaters, where the saltiness changes with the tide and the season.
Mudskippers on the mudflats of the Sundarbans cope with river water, sea water and air on the same day.
explanations.art: A silver hilsa swimming from blue sea water on the left, through a mixed green-blue estuary, into a brown monsoon river on the right.

explanations.concept: Desert animals spend almost no water
explanations.definition: A desert animal survives by losing very little water. Some never drink, and live on the water in their food and on metabolic water, which is water their cells make from food.
explanations.description: When a cell uses food for energy, the hydrogen in the food joins with oxygen and makes new water. This is metabolic water. You make about a tumbler of it a day. The kangaroo rat of the North American deserts lives on it. In 1948 Bodil and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen and their co-workers showed that kangaroo rats can live on dry grain with nothing to drink. Every 100 grams of dry barley gives the rat about 54 grams of water made in her cells. That is enough only because she loses so little. Her urine is nearly five times as strong as the strongest human urine. Her droppings are almost dry. Her nose is cool inside, so water in her warm breath turns back to liquid there before the breath leaves. And she spends the hot day in a closed burrow, where the air is cooler and damper. In the Thar desert, Indian desert jirds and spiny-tailed lizards also shelter in burrows. A camel is too big to hide, so she saves water in other ways. Her hump is fat, and it holds no store of water. When she is short of water she lets her body warm up, from about 34 degrees Celsius at dawn to about 41 degrees in the afternoon. Then she cools off at night without sweating. She can lose water equal to about 30 parts in 100 of her body weight and still walk. Most mammals are in danger at less than half that. When she reaches water, she can drink back about a third of her body weight in one visit. For a large camel that is well over 100 litres.
examples: Kangaroo rat: dry seeds, no drinking, very strong urine, a cool nose and a closed burrow.
Camel: a body temperature that swings by several degrees, dry dung, strong urine and a huge drink when water is found.
Darkling beetles and other desert insects send out nitrogen waste as dry uric acid and take back water from their droppings before these leave.
explanations.art: A split picture of the Thar at noon: a camel standing on a dune above ground, and below ground a small rodent curled in a cool burrow with the entrance plugged with sand.

explanations.concept: Salt glands: how seabirds and sea turtles drink the sea
explanations.definition: A salt gland is an organ that pumps salt out of the blood as a liquid much saltier than sea water. With salt glands, an animal can drink sea water and still gain water.
explanations.description: A bird's kidneys cannot make urine as salty as the sea. Yet gulls, cormorants and albatrosses live at sea for months and drink sea water. In 1958 Knut Schmidt-Nielsen and his co-workers found out how. They gave sea water to cormorants and collected clear drops that ran from the birds' nostrils and off the tip of the beak. The drops were saltier than sea water. They came from a pair of glands in the head, just above the eyes. The cells of these glands pump salt out of the blood, and a little water follows it. A seabird shakes the drops off her beak. Sea turtles have salt glands that empty beside the eyes. An olive ridley turtle laying her eggs on a beach in Odisha seems to weep thick tears. She is getting rid of salt. Marine iguanas sneeze their salt out. Whales and dolphins have no salt glands. They get most of their water from the fish and squid they eat and from metabolic water, and their kidneys make strong urine.
examples: A gull on the beach at Rameswaram shakes her head now and then, and clear salty drops fly off her beak.
Olive ridley turtles nest in huge numbers at Gahirmatha and Rushikulya in Odisha, and their salt tears can be seen on the beach.
Sharks have a salt gland too, near the end of the gut.
explanations.art: A cormorant on a rock by the sea with a clear drop hanging from the tip of her beak, and a small cut-away drawing showing a gland above her eye.

explanations.definition: Every living body balances water and salt, with or without kidneys. One-celled creatures, worms, insects and even some plants each have their own way.
explanations.description: A Paramecium is a single cell living in pond water. They are saltier inside than the pond, so water enters by osmosis without stopping. Left alone, the cell would swell and burst. So they collect the incoming water in a small bag called a contractile vacuole, and squeeze it out through the membrane every few seconds. An earthworm has small coiled tubes, called nephridia, in almost every ring of their body. Some kinds of earthworm have one pair in each ring, and the common Indian earthworm has many tiny ones. Each tube takes in liquid from inside the body and takes back what is useful. The rest leaves through the skin or into the gut. An insect has fine threads called Malpighian tubules, which hang in the blood and empty into the gut. Cells of the tubule pump salts into it, water follows, and wastes are carried along. Then the last part of the gut takes most of the water and salt back. What leaves is nearly dry. The grey mangrove trees at Pichavaram stand in brackish water. They take in some salt with the water. Glands on their leaves push that salt out again, and you can see the crystals on the leaves on a dry day.
examples: Paramecium in a pond: a bag that bails water out every few seconds.
Earthworm: small coiled tubes in nearly every ring of the body.
Cockroach: threads that empty into the gut, and a gut that takes the water back.
Grey mangrove: glands on the leaf that push out salt.
explanations.art: Four small drawings in a row: a Paramecium with a star-shaped vacuole, one ring of an earthworm with a coiled tube, a cockroach's gut with thin threads attached, and a mangrove leaf with salt crystals on it.

explanations.concept: Losing water and salt together: why ORS has sugar in it
explanations.definition: ORS is a drink of clean water with measured salt and sugar. The gut takes in salt much faster when sugar is there with it, and water follows the salt.
explanations.description: Sweat and loose motions carry away both water and salt. In bad diarrhoea, such as cholera, a person can lose many litres in a day, and that can kill. For a long time the only treatment was salt water dripped into a vein through a needle. In the early 1960s the American biochemist Robert Crane described a carrier in the wall of the gut. It takes sodium, from salt, into the gut cells, but only together with glucose, a simple sugar. Once the sodium is inside the body, water follows it by osmosis. This carrier keeps working even during cholera. So a drink with the right amounts of salt and sugar can put water back into a person through the mouth. In 1953 the Kolkata doctor Hemendra Nath Chatterjee reported in a medical journal that he had treated 186 cholera patients this way. Few doctors took notice. In 1971, during the Bangladesh war, cholera spread through the refugee camps of West Bengal and the drip bottles ran out. Dr Dilip Mahalanabis and his team had families give the patients a drink of salt, glucose and water. More than 3,000 patients were treated. In the camps using this drink, about 4 patients in 100 died. With drips alone the figure had been about 30 in 100. The amounts matter. Too much salt is harmful. Too much sugar holds water in the gut by osmosis and makes diarrhoea worse, which is why soft drinks and sweet juices are not ORS.
examples: Home ORS: one litre of clean water, six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt.
Salted lime juice with a little sugar, thin salted rice kanji and tender coconut water all give water with some salt and sugar.
For anyone ill with loose motions, a packet of ORS from a chemist or a health centre is the right choice, and a doctor should be asked.
explanations.art: A health worker in a cotton sari stirring salt and sugar into a large steel pot of water, with a mother and child waiting with a tumbler.

explanations.concept: Did the kidney's filter first appear in fresh water?
explanations.description: A kidney filters a huge amount of liquid out of the blood and then takes nearly all of it back. That looks wasteful. Why would such an organ ever appear? Scientists do not agree. The answer depends on where the first animals with backbones lived, more than 450 million years ago, and the fossils do not settle it easily.
examples: A river fish uses her filters to send out a flood of water, which fits the first view below.
Hagfish have filters in their kidneys and live only in the sea, which fits the second view.
Some sea fish, such as the toadfish, have lost their filters altogether and make urine without them.

perspectives.who: Homer Smith, American kidney scientist, in his book From Fish to Philosopher (1953)
perspectives.explanation: The first animals with backbones lived in fresh water. Water poured into them by osmosis. The filter appeared as a way to bail that water out. Later animals, on land and in the sea, kept the filter and added ways to take water back.

perspectives.who: James Robertson, British zoologist (1957), and many fossil scientists today
perspectives.explanation: The oldest fossils of animals with backbones are found in rocks laid down in the sea. Their living relatives, the hagfish, live only in the sea. So the filter probably appeared in the sea, and it was not built for bailing out fresh water.

A filter is useful in any water. It lets the body throw out everything small and take back only what is wanted, including wastes the body has never met before. It did not need fresh water as a reason.

explanations.art: An ancient jawless armoured fish drawn twice, once in a river and once in the sea, with a question mark between the two.

agreed.text: Water crosses cell membranes through water doors called aquaporins, and osmosis decides the direction.
agreed.evidence: In 1992 Peter Agre's team put the protein into frog eggs, which normally take in water very slowly. In plain water the eggs with the protein swelled and burst within minutes. Agre shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2003.

agreed.text: Bony sea fish drink sea water and send the salt out through their gills.
agreed.evidence: Homer Smith showed in 1930 that sea fish swallow sea water and absorb most of it. Ancel Keys and Edward Willmer described the salt-moving cells in eel gills in 1932.

agreed.text: Some desert rodents live their whole lives without drinking.
agreed.evidence: In 1948 Bodil and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen and their co-workers kept kangaroo rats on dry grain with no water. They measured every gram of water the rats made and lost.

agreed.text: The kidney concentrates urine by making its own deep part very salty.
agreed.evidence: In 1951 Wirz, Hargitay and Kuhn froze slices of rat kidney and found that the tissue becomes steadily more concentrated from the outside to the deepest tip.

agreed.text: Seabirds and sea turtles get rid of extra salt through glands in the head, and the kidneys are not involved.
agreed.evidence: In 1958 Knut Schmidt-Nielsen and his co-workers gave sea water to cormorants and collected drops from the beak that were saltier than sea water.

agreed.text: A drink of water, salt and glucose can replace the water lost in severe diarrhoea.
agreed.evidence: In 1971 Dilip Mahalanabis and his team treated more than 3,000 cholera patients in refugee camps in West Bengal. About 4 in 100 died, against about 30 in 100 with drips alone.

challenging.context: This card is about a very old belief: that a camel carries a store of water inside her hump.
challenging.claim: A camel stores water in her hump.
challenging.who: A common belief, at least two thousand years old
challenging.for: A camel can walk for a week or more in the heat without drinking. Her hump shrinks and flops over on a long journey. Both facts look like a water tank being emptied.
challenging.against: The hump is fat, which is a store of food. In 1953 and 1954 Knut and Bodil Schmidt-Nielsen and their team studied camels in the Sahara and found no water store anywhere in the body. A camel lasts because she loses water slowly and can bear losing a great deal.

challenging.context: This card is about a claim made by a French doctor who crossed the Atlantic Ocean alone in a rubber boat in 1952.
challenging.claim: A person lost at sea should drink small amounts of sea water from the first day.
challenging.who: Alain Bombard, French doctor, after his voyage in 1952
challenging.for: Bombard said he drank small amounts of sea water, and the liquid pressed from raw fish, and lived for 65 days. He argued that a little sea water, started early, is better than none.
challenging.against: Human urine cannot hold salt as strongly as sea water does, so each drink costs more water than it gives. Navies and sea rescue services advise people never to drink sea water. Other sailors who tried Bombard's method reported that they needed fresh water as well.

challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that every fish drinks water all day long.
challenging.claim: All fish drink water all the time.
challenging.for: A fish's mouth opens and shuts all day, and water keeps going in. Bony sea fish really do swallow sea water steadily.
challenging.against: Most of the water a fish takes into her mouth goes out over the gills, for breathing. A river fish swallows hardly any, because water is already entering her by osmosis. Sharks do not need to drink either.

challenging.context: This card is about the idea that drinking more water is always better for you.
challenging.claim: You cannot drink too much water. The more you drink, the healthier your kidneys are.
challenging.for: Too little water does cause harm, such as headaches and kidney stones. Healthy kidneys can send out a lot of extra water.
challenging.against: Kidneys can send out only about one litre of extra water an hour. A person who drinks much faster than that for hours makes their blood too watery, and their brain cells swell. In a study of runners in the 2002 Boston Marathon, about 13 runners in 100 finished with too little sodium in their blood, mostly from drinking too much.

challenging.context: This card is about the white part of a bird's dropping. Textbooks say it is uric acid. A newer study disagrees.
challenging.claim: The white part of a bird's dropping is not uric acid by the time it leaves the bird.
challenging.who: Nicholas Crouch, Vincent Lynch and Julia Clarke, scientists in the United States, in 2019
challenging.for: They tested the white part of droppings from six kinds of birds with X-rays. They found no uric acid. They found other white solids, such as ammonium urate and struvite. They think microbes in the bird's gut change the uric acid before it leaves.
challenging.against: Older studies of many more kinds of birds did report uric acid. Six kinds of birds is a small sample. Everyone agrees that birds make uric acid in the body, and the argument is only about what happens to it on the way out.

how_we_found_out.context: A kangaroo rat never drinks, and a camel can walk for a week without water. How do they do it? This is how two scientists found out.
how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, travellers said that a camel carries a tank of water inside her, in the hump or in the stomach. It seemed obvious. An animal who goes without drinking must have a store. Bodil Schmidt-Nielsen grew up in Copenhagen, where both her parents studied how bodies work. In the 1940s she and her husband Knut went to the desert in Arizona to study kangaroo rats, small rodents who never seem to drink. They kept the rats on dry grain with no water at all. They measured the water in the grain, in the air the rats breathed out, in their urine and in their droppings. The rats stayed healthy. The sums showed where the water came from. The rats' cells made it from the food, and the rats lost almost none. The results were published in 1948. In 1953 and 1954 the couple and their co-workers lived in the Sahara and did the same careful measuring on camels. They found no water tank. The hump was fat. A camel lasts because she loses water slowly, lets her body warm up by day, and can bear a very large loss.
how_we_found_out.who: Bodil Schmidt-Nielsen and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen, with their co-workers A. Brokaw and H. Schneiderman for the kangaroo rats, and S. A. Jarnum and T. R. Houpt for the camels
how_we_found_out.when: The kangaroo rat study was published in 1948. The camel studies were done in the Sahara in 1953 and 1954 and published in 1956 and 1957.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That an animal who goes without drinking must carry a hidden store of water, such as a camel's hump. The Schmidt-Nielsens measured all the water going into and out of these animals. They found no store. The animals make some water from their food and lose very little.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist of the 1940s in a desert field tent, weighing a small kangaroo rat in a tin on a balance, with a notebook of figures beside her.

big_questions.q: A sea fish has water all around her and is always short of it. So what does it mean to have water?
big_questions.hint: Think about the sailor too. Is water you cannot use still water, for you?

big_questions.q: Your kidneys never push water. They move salt, and the water follows. So who is moving the water?
big_questions.hint: In the Salted Cucumber Test, did you take the water out of the cucumber? Did the salt? Did the water move by itself?

big_questions.q: A hilsa, a girl and a gecko send out the same nitrogen as three different wastes. What makes a thing waste?
big_questions.hint: The ammonia a fish lets go is taken up by water plants as food. Farmers buy urea as fertiliser.

big_questions.q: A hilsa changes how her gills and kidneys work when she swims from the sea into a river. Is she still the same fish?
big_questions.hint: Which parts of her changed, and which stayed? You also changed when you stopped being a baby.

big_questions.q: A drink of salt, sugar and water costs a few rupees and has saved millions of lives. Why did doctors take so long to trust it?
big_questions.hint: Dr Chatterjee wrote about it in 1953. It was widely used only after 1971. Think about whose ideas are listened to, and what counts as proper medicine.

big_questions.q: Nearly all the water on Earth is sea water, and no land animal can live on it. So who makes the fresh water we drink?
big_questions.hint: Think about where rain comes from, and what the Sun leaves behind in the sea.

story.title: The Good Water
story.note: A made-up story. Thoothukudi is a real port town in Tamil Nadu, and its salt pans are real. Muthulakshmi, Selvam, Aachi and Mariammal Athai are imagined. It is true that a sea fish put into fresh water takes in water through her gills and is soon in danger. It is true that raw sea salt dissolved in water, about 35 grams to a litre, can keep small sea animals alive for some hours. People who keep sea fish for longer use a measured sea-salt mix and never plain kitchen salt. Wild animals borrowed from the shore should go back the same day, as they do here.
text: On Friday evening, when the tide was far out, Muthulakshmi and her aunt waded into the shallows beyond the fishing harbour with a hand net and a blue plastic drum. Tomorrow was Sea Day at school. Every child in Class 6 was to bring something from the shore and tell the others about it.

Mariammal Athai knew where the small ones hid. By the time the lamps came on along the harbour wall, the drum held four silver fish with yellow stripes, each no longer than a finger, and two hermit crabs in borrowed shells. 'One day only,' said Athai. 'Tomorrow evening they go back to the same place.' Muthu promised.
They carried the drum home between them and set it on the veranda. Selvam, who was six and Athai's son, lay on his stomach beside it until he was called three times for dinner.

Aachi came in late from the salt pans. She had raked salt there for forty years, and her hands showed it. The skin of her palms was thick and split, with white lines where the brine had dried. She sat on the step and rubbed coconut oil into them, as she did every night, and looked into the drum. 'Pretty,' she said. 'Thirsty work, living in that.' Muthu did not know what she meant and was too sleepy to ask.

Selvam woke before anyone else. He went straight to the drum. In the grey light the water looked worse than it had at night. There was sand at the bottom and a shred of weed, and it smelled of the harbour. The fish hung in the middle of it, hardly moving.

Selvam knew about water. In their street the sweet water came on Tuesdays and Fridays, and everyone queued for it with pots. That water was for drinking and for rice. Nobody wasted a tumbler of it. It was the good water. And here were four fish and two crabs, guests in the house, sitting in dirty water from the harbour.

He fetched the steel bucket and filled it from the big pot of sweet water in the kitchen, tumbler by tumbler, without spilling. He caught the fish one at a time in the tumbler, which took a long while, and tipped each one gently into the bucket. He lifted the crabs across by their shells. Then he dragged the blue drum to the edge of the veranda and poured the harbour water into the drain. He sat down beside the bucket, very pleased, to watch his guests enjoy themselves.
That was how Muthu found him. He was not pleased any more.
'They don't like it,' he said. His voice was small.

Muthu knelt and looked. The fish were not hanging quietly now. Their gill covers were opening and closing fast, far too fast. One had tilted to the side and kept correcting herself. Another lay near the bottom, leaning against the steel. Both crabs had pulled so far into their shells that the shells looked empty.
'What did you put them in?'
'The good water. From the pot.' He began to cry. 'The other was dirty.'

Muthu's first thought was air. She swirled the water with her hand to stir some in. The fish went on gasping. Her second thought was the bucket, but it was the clean one, the one for rice. There was nothing in that water at all. It was the cleanest water in the house.
There was nothing in that water at all.

She thought of Aachi on the back step every March, laying sardines in a basket with a fistful of salt between each layer. By the next morning the basket always sat in a puddle, and the fish had gone thin and stiff. 'The salt calls the water out,' Aachi said every year. Muthu had thought it was only a way of talking. And she thought of the chickpeas her mother left in a bowl of water at night. By morning they were twice the size and tight in their skins.

The water went to whichever side had more in it. These fish had been made in the sea and they were salty inside, though not as salty as the sea. And she and Selvam had put them in water with nothing in it. The water would be going into them now. Through the gills, most likely, where the skin was thinnest. They were filling up like the chickpeas.
The sea was twenty minutes away at a run, and twenty back with a full pot. She looked at the fish leaning on the steel and ran to wake her grandmother instead.
Aachi listened without sitting up. Then she got up faster than Muthu had seen her move in years. 'You want me to make sea,' she said. 'I have been unmaking it for forty years.'

She took the bag of grey pan salt from under the kitchen shelf. It was the coarse kind she brought home from work, not the white powder from the shop. 'The sea is thinner than people think,' she said. 'At the pans we wait weeks for the sun to thicken it. For a bucket like this, three of my fistfuls, and a little more.' She would not put it in the bucket. She stirred the salt into a separate pot of water until the last grain had gone, then touched one finger to it and to her tongue. 'More.' Another pinch. She tasted again and nodded. 'That is the tide coming in.'

'Now slowly. A body does not like to be surprised.' She scooped half the sweet water out of the bucket, and Muthu poured the new water in, one tumbler at a time, with a count of twenty between tumblers. Selvam counted for her. He had stopped crying so that he could count properly.

For a long time nothing changed. Then the fish near the bottom lifted off the steel. The tilted one stopped tilting. Their gill covers slowed, a little and then a little more. When the sun reached the veranda, one hermit crab put out two legs and an eye on a stalk and walked across the bottom of the bucket.
They took the bucket to Sea Day on the back of Athai's cycle, with a wet cloth over the top. Three of the fish were swimming. The fourth swam too, but slowly, and Muthu watched her all morning.

In the evening the tide was out again. The three of them waded to the same place, and Selvam was allowed to tip the bucket. The fish were gone before the water had finished pouring. The crabs sat on the sand for a moment, then walked off in different directions.
Selvam stood looking at the place where they had been. Then he bent down, scooped up a handful of the sea and tasted it. He made a terrible face.
'Good water,' he said, and spat.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Selvam gives the sea fish the cleanest water in the house, and it nearly kills them. A sea fish is less salty than the sea but far saltier than tap water. In fresh water, water moves into her through her gills by osmosis, and her body is set up to push salt out and keep water in, which is now the wrong way round. Muthulakshmi works this out from two things she has seen at home: salt drawing water out of sardines, and chickpeas swelling in plain water. Water that is good for one body can be dangerous for another, because what matters is the difference between the inside and the outside.
ask: Water with nothing in it harmed the sea fish. Which way was water moving, and why?
Would a pond fish, such as a rohu, have been harmed by the same bucket of tap water? Why or why not?
Why is it safer to change the saltiness of a fish's water slowly than all at once?
Sardines packed in salt lose water. Chickpeas in plain water gain it. What one rule explains both?
Is there such a thing as water that is good for every living being?

games.title: Three Clues: whose water problem is this?
games.context: This is a guessing game about how different living beings balance water and salt. Each card gives three clues about one being, from hard to easy. The sooner you guess who it is, the more points you get.

printables.title: 16 clue cards to cut out (three clues on the front, the answer on the back)

items.f: Clue 1: Water enters me by osmosis all day, and I hardly ever drink. Clue 2: I pass a lot of very weak urine. Clue 3: Cells in my gills pump salt in from pond water.
items.b: A river or pond fish, such as a rohu. She is saltier than the water around her, so water keeps coming in.

items.f: Clue 1: I live in water and I am always in danger of drying out. Clue 2: I drink all day and pass very little urine. Clue 3: Cells in my gills pump salt out into the sea.
items.b: A bony sea fish, such as a mackerel. She is less salty than the sea, so water keeps leaving her.

items.f: Clue 1: I keep a waste in my blood on purpose. Clue 2: That waste is urea, and it makes me as concentrated as the sea. Clue 3: I have a skeleton of cartilage and many rows of teeth.
items.b: A shark. With so much urea in her blood, water does not leave her by osmosis, and she does not need to drink.

items.f: Clue 1: Twice in my life I reverse the salt pumps in my gills. Clue 2: I grow up in the sea and lay my eggs in a river. Clue 3: In Bengal I am called ilish, and on the Godavari I am called pulasa.
items.b: A hilsa. In the estuary her gills change from pumping salt out to pumping salt in.

items.f: Clue 1: Most of my water is made inside my own cells. Clue 2: My urine is nearly five times as strong as the strongest human urine. Clue 3: I am a small hopping rodent of the North American desert, and I never drink.
items.b: A kangaroo rat. She makes about 54 grams of water from 100 grams of dry barley, and loses very little.

items.f: Clue 1: When water is short I let my body warm up by several degrees during the day. Clue 2: I can lose nearly a third of my body weight in water and still walk. Clue 3: My hump is fat. It holds no store of water.
items.b: A camel. By warming up in the day and cooling at night, she avoids sweating away many litres of water.

items.f: Clue 1: My kidneys cannot make urine as salty as what I drink. Clue 2: Salty drops run from my nostrils to the tip of my beak. Clue 3: I fly over the sea for weeks and drink sea water.
items.b: A seabird, such as a gull or a cormorant. Salt glands above her eyes pump out liquid saltier than the sea.

items.f: Clue 1: People say I cry when I come ashore. Clue 2: The thick tears are salt leaving my body. Clue 3: I have a shell and flippers, and I lay my eggs on beaches in Odisha.
items.b: A sea turtle, such as an olive ridley. Her salt glands empty beside her eyes.

items.f: Clue 1: My nitrogen waste leaves as a white solid. Clue 2: I lose only a few drops of water with it. Clue 3: I run up walls near the tube light and catch moths.
items.b: A house gecko. The white cap on a gecko's dropping is nitrogen waste made from uric acid.

items.f: Clue 1: I change my nitrogen waste as I grow up. Clue 2: When young I let ammonia out through my gills. As an adult I make urea. Clue 3: I begin life with a tail in a pond and end it hopping on land.
items.b: A frog. A tadpole can wash ammonia away in pond water. A frog on land cannot spare that much water.

items.f: Clue 1: My strongest urine is about four times as concentrated as my blood. Clue 2: A hormone from my brain tells my kidneys how much water to take back. Clue 3: I am reading this card.
items.b: A human. ADH, the water-saving hormone, opens water doors in the collecting ducts of the kidneys.

items.f: Clue 1: I have no kidney, and I am not even two cells. Clue 2: A bag inside me fills with water and squeezes it out every few seconds. Clue 3: I am a slipper-shaped creature of pond water, seen with a microscope.
items.b: A Paramecium. Water enters the cell by osmosis all the time, and the contractile vacuole bails it out.

items.f: Clue 1: I have small coiled tubes for waste in nearly every ring of my body. Clue 2: My skin must stay damp, or I die. Clue 3: I tunnel through garden soil and come up after rain.
items.b: An earthworm. Each coiled tube, called a nephridium, takes back what is useful and lets the rest go.

items.f: Clue 1: Fine threads floating in my blood collect my waste and empty it into my gut. Clue 2: My gut takes the water back, so my droppings are nearly dry. Clue 3: I have six legs and run under the kitchen sink at night.
items.b: A cockroach. The threads are called Malpighian tubules, and the waste leaves as dry uric acid.

items.f: Clue 1: I have no kidneys, no blood and no mouth, yet I push salt out. Clue 2: On a dry day you can see salt crystals on my leaves. Clue 3: I am a tree standing in brackish water at Pichavaram.
items.b: A grey mangrove. Glands on the leaves push out salt that came in with the water.

items.f: Clue 1: I live in the sea, but I have no salt glands and I do not rely on drinking sea water. Clue 2: My water comes from the fish and squid I eat, and from my own cells. Clue 3: I breathe air through a blowhole.
items.b: A dolphin or a whale. The fish she eats are less salty than the sea, and her kidneys make strong urine.

rules: For 2 or more players, or for one player alone. You need the 16 cards, a paper and a pencil for the score.
Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the clues facing up. Cover the pile with a blank piece of paper.
With 2 players: one player is the reader and picks up the top card, keeping the back hidden. The reader reads Clue 1 aloud. The other player has one guess.
A right guess after Clue 1 scores 3 points. If the guess is wrong, the reader reads Clue 2, and a right guess now scores 2 points. A right guess after Clue 3 scores 1 point.
After the guess, the reader turns the card over and reads the back aloud. Then the players swap jobs.
With 3 or more players: take turns to be the reader. After each clue, every other player may make one guess, going round the circle. The first right guess scores.
The game ends when all 16 cards have been used. The player with the most points wins.
Alone: slide the blank paper down the top card to show one clue at a time. Say your guess aloud before you turn the card. Try to score more than 30 out of 48.

flow.say: Each card has three clues about one living being. The first clue is the hardest. Guess as early as you dare.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the rules. Play two cards for practice.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Clues. Here you cut out the cards and learn how a turn goes.
flow.parent: The reader must keep the back of the card hidden. If the words on a card are new, read the back slowly and talk about it for a moment.

flow.do: 1. Play through all the cards, swapping jobs after each one. 2. Read every back aloud, even after a right guess. 3. Keep the score on paper.
flow.say: Listen for which way the water is moving. Is it coming into this body, or leaving it?
flow.kid: Play all the cards. Swap jobs each time. Always read the back aloud. Keep the score.
flow.context: This is the playing step of Three Clues. Each card gives three clues about one living being and its water problem.
flow.parent: A guess of the right kind of animal counts. 'A sea fish' is right for the mackerel card, and 'a lizard' is right for the gecko card.

check.q: A card says: 'I live in water and I am always in danger of drying out.' Who is it?
options: A pond fish
A bony sea fish
A frog
check.why: A bony sea fish is less salty than the sea, so water leaves her by osmosis all day. A pond fish has the opposite problem, with water coming in. This is a moment in the game, and a wrong guess simply means hearing the next clue.

flow.do: 1. Spread all 16 cards with the answers facing up. 2. Sort them into three groups: water keeps coming in, water keeps leaving, and both at different times. 3. Talk about any card you disagree on.
flow.say: Let's sort them. For which of these is water always coming in? For which is it always leaving? Which have both problems?
flow.kid: Lay out all the cards. Sort them: water coming in, water leaving, or both. Say why for each.
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Clues. Here you sort the 16 living beings by their water problem.
flow.parent: Coming in: the pond fish, the Paramecium and the tadpole. Leaving: the sea fish, the kangaroo rat, the camel, the gecko, the cockroach and the human. Both, at different times: the hilsa and the frog. The shark hardly has either problem. The others can be argued, and arguing is the point.

games.title: Cross the Thar: a board game with water beans
games.context: This is a board game about saving water in a desert. You are a desert animal with only 7 beans of water. You choose two water-saving tricks and try to cross 24 squares to the oasis before your water runs out.

printables.title: 24 squares for the track (draw them in a line or a spiral, or cut them out and lay them in order)
items: 1. Dawn. The air is cool. Nothing happens.
2. You pass urine. Lose 2 beans. With Strong Urine, lose 1. With Paste Waste, lose 0.
3. A hot wind dries your breath. Lose 2 beans. With Cool Nose, lose 1.
4. You find dry seeds. Your cells make water from them. Gain 1 bean.
5. The noon sun. Lose 3 beans. With Burrow by Day, lose 0.
6. You leave droppings. Lose 1 bean. With Dry Droppings, lose 0.
7. You pass urine. Lose 2 beans. With Strong Urine, lose 1. With Paste Waste, lose 0.
8. The afternoon heat makes you sweat. Lose 3 beans. With Warm-Up Body, lose 1.
9. You find a juicy plant. Gain 2 beans.
10. The noon sun. Lose 3 beans. With Burrow by Day, lose 0.
11. A hot wind dries your breath. Lose 2 beans. With Cool Nose, lose 1.
12. Night. The air is cool. Nothing happens.
13. You pass urine. Lose 2 beans. With Strong Urine, lose 1. With Paste Waste, lose 0.
14. You find dry seeds. Your cells make water from them. Gain 1 bean.
15. The afternoon heat makes you sweat. Lose 3 beans. With Warm-Up Body, lose 1.
16. You leave droppings. Lose 1 bean. With Dry Droppings, lose 0.
17. The noon sun. Lose 3 beans. With Burrow by Day, lose 0.
18. A dust storm. Lose 1 bean. No trick helps.
19. A hot wind dries your breath. Lose 2 beans. With Cool Nose, lose 1.
20. You pass urine. Lose 2 beans. With Strong Urine, lose 1. With Paste Waste, lose 0.
21. You find dry seeds. Your cells make water from them. Gain 1 bean.
22. The afternoon heat makes you sweat. Lose 3 beans. With Warm-Up Body, lose 1.
23. The noon sun. Lose 3 beans. With Burrow by Day, lose 0.
24. The oasis. You have crossed the desert. Drink.

printables.title: 6 trick cards (the real animal who uses the trick is on the back)

items.f: Strong Urine. On a urine square, lose 1 bean and not 2.
items.b: A kangaroo rat's urine is nearly five times as strong as the strongest human urine. The same waste leaves in much less water.

items.f: Cool Nose. On a hot wind square, lose 1 bean and not 2.
items.b: A kangaroo rat's and a camel's breath passes over cool walls inside the nose. Water vapour turns back to liquid there and stays in the body.

items.f: Burrow by Day. On a noon sun square, lose no beans.
items.b: Desert jirds, gerbils and spiny-tailed lizards of the Thar spend the hottest hours in burrows, where the air is cooler and damper.

items.f: Dry Droppings. On a droppings square, lose no beans.
items.b: A camel's dung is so dry that it can be burned as fuel almost at once. Her gut takes back nearly all the water.

items.f: Warm-Up Body. On an afternoon heat square, lose 1 bean and not 3.
items.b: A camel short of water lets her body warm from about 34 to about 41 degrees Celsius by day and cools at night. She does not need to sweat that heat away.

items.f: Paste Waste. On a urine square, lose no beans. But making paste costs energy, so you start with 6 beans and not 7.
items.b: Lizards, snakes, birds and insects send out nitrogen waste as a paste made from uric acid. It needs very little water, but more energy to make.

rules: For 1 to 4 players. You need the 24 squares, the 6 trick cards, one die, a button for each player and about 40 dry beans.
Lay the 6 trick cards face up where everyone can read them. Each player chooses 2 tricks and writes them down. Two players may choose the same trick.
Each player takes 7 beans of water. A player who chose Paste Waste takes 6.
On your turn, roll the die and move your button that many squares. Read the square aloud and do what it says, using your tricks.
If you have no beans left, your animal has dried out. Go back to before square 1, take your starting beans again, and you may change one of your tricks.
The first player to reach square 24 wins. You do not need an exact roll.
Alone: cross the desert three times with one pair of tricks and count how many times you arrive. Then try another pair. Find the pair that gets you across most often.
A short game: play one crossing each and compare the beans you have left.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with 24 numbered squares drawn in a spiral, each with a short line of writing, a die, two buttons and a heap of dry beans beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw or lay out the 24 squares. Each player takes a button and 7 beans.

setup.art: Six small cards laid face up in two rows with names such as Burrow by Day and Cool Nose, and a child pointing at two of them.
setup.caption: 2. Read the six trick cards. Choose two and write them down.

setup.art: A child rolling a die beside the spiral board and handing three beans back to the heap after landing on a square marked noon sun.
setup.caption: 3. Roll, move, read the square and pay or gain beans. Reach square 24 before your beans run out.

flow.do: 1. Draw the 24 squares on a large sheet, or cut them out and lay them in a line. 2. Read the six trick cards aloud, fronts and backs. 3. Each player chooses two tricks and takes their beans.
flow.say: You are a desert animal with seven beans of water. Which two tricks will get you across? Why those two?
flow.kid: Lay out the squares. Read the six trick cards. Choose two tricks. Take your beans.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cross the Thar. Here you set out the board and choose two water-saving tricks.
flow.parent: Let your child choose freely, even a weak pair. Running dry and changing a trick is how the game teaches.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll, move and read the square aloud. 2. Pay or gain beans. 3. A player with no beans goes back to the start and may change one trick. 4. Play until someone reaches square 24.
flow.say: Read your square aloud. Does one of your tricks help here? How many beans do you pay?
flow.kid: Roll and move. Read your square aloud. Pay or gain beans. If you run out, go back and change a trick.
flow.context: This is the playing step of Cross the Thar. Each square of the desert costs or gives beans of water.
flow.parent: With no useful tricks, an animal gets across only about one time in four. With Burrow by Day and Warm-Up Body together, it is about four times in five.

check.q: In Cross the Thar, which squares take the most water from an animal with no tricks?
options: The urine squares
The noon sun and afternoon heat squares
The droppings squares
check.why: Heat costs 3 beans each time, and there are seven such squares. Keeping cool by sweating is the biggest loss of water for a desert animal who stays out in the day. This is a moment in the game, and you can check it by counting the squares.

flow.do: 1. Ask which trick saved the most beans, and why. 2. Count the squares each trick helps on. 3. Ask which real animal uses each trick, and turn the cards over to check.
flow.say: Which trick mattered most? Count how many squares it helps on. Which real animal uses it?
flow.kid: Which trick saved the most beans? Count the squares it helps on. Turn the cards over and read the backs.
flow.context: This is the last step of Cross the Thar. Here you work out which water-saving trick matters most, and why.

ask.q: A camel cannot use Burrow by Day. Why not, and what does she use?
good: She is far too big to dig a burrow.
She lets her body warm up in the day, so she does not have to sweat.

flow.parent: Burrow by Day helps on four squares and saves 3 beans each time, which is more than any other trick. That matches real deserts. Most small desert animals spend the day underground.

experiments.title: The Salted Cucumber Test: does more salt pull out more water?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sprinkle different amounts of salt on cucumber slices and measure the liquid that collects in each bowl. You will find out what salt does to living cells, and whether twice the salt brings out twice the water.
experiments.question: When salt is sprinkled on cucumber slices, does liquid come out of them? Does twice as much salt bring out twice as much liquid?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Four bowls each hold 15 cucumber slices. Bowl 1 gets no salt. Bowl 2 gets a quarter of a teaspoon, bowl 3 gets half a teaspoon and bowl 4 gets one whole teaspoon. After 18 minutes, how many millilitres of liquid will be in each bowl? Write a number for each bowl, and write the reason for your guess.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the amount of salt. Cut all the slices from the same cucumbers, about as thick as a 5 rupee coin, and put 15 in each bowl. Use four bowls of the same size. Toss every bowl 10 times, including the bowl with no salt. Wait the same 18 minutes for all four. Bowl 1 has no salt, so it shows how much liquid comes out from cutting alone.
results_table: How a slice feels when I bend it

materials.item: medium cucumbers, fresh and firm, about 400 grams in all
small steel bowls of the same size
fine table salt, about 2 teaspoons
a teaspoon, a steel plate and a butter knife, for measuring the salt
a knife and a chopping board, for a grown-up
a 10 millilitre medicine measuring cup with marks, or a 5 millilitre syrup spoon or dropper
a clean spoon for tossing and for holding back the slices
a phone timer, four slips of paper, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the slicing with the sharp knife.

schedule.what: Guess. Slice the cucumbers into four bowls. Salt three of them. Wait 18 minutes. Measure the liquid in each bowl and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all four bowls. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each bowl. Then write three sentences: what you guessed and why, what you measured, and what you think moved the water.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: liquid in each bowl after 18 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Four small steel bowls in a row on a kitchen counter, each holding a heap of thin cucumber slices, with paper slips numbered 1 to 4 in front of them.
setup.caption: 1. Put 15 thin cucumber slices in each of four bowls.

setup.art: A steel plate with one level teaspoon of salt divided into four equal small heaps with a butter knife, and a child's hand sprinkling one heap over a bowl of cucumber slices.
setup.caption: 2. Bowl 1 gets no salt. Bowls 2, 3 and 4 get a quarter, a half and one whole teaspoon.

setup.art: A child tipping a steel bowl over a small plastic medicine cup with millilitre marks, holding the cucumber slices back with a spoon while clear liquid runs into the cup.
setup.caption: 3. After 18 minutes, tip the liquid from each bowl into a medicine cup and read the millilitres.

flow.do: 1. Read the question aloud and ask for a guess for each bowl, with a reason. 2. Write the guesses in the table. 3. Slice both cucumbers into rounds about as thick as a 5 rupee coin. 4. Your child counts 15 slices into each bowl and numbers the bowls 1 to 4.
flow.say: How much liquid do you think each bowl will have after 18 minutes? Give me a number for each. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the liquid in each bowl. Say why. Ask a grown-up to slice the cucumbers. Count 15 slices into each bowl.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Salted Cucumber Test. Here you guess, and you get four bowls of slices ready.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect no liquid at all, or expect the salt to soak liquid up. Leave the skin on the cucumber. Slices of even thickness matter more than exact size.

flow.do: 1. Level one teaspoon of salt and tip it on a plate. 2. Divide the heap into four equal parts with the butter knife. 3. Toss bowl 1 ten times with the clean spoon, with no salt. 4. Sprinkle one part on bowl 2, two parts on bowl 3 and a fresh level teaspoon on bowl 4. 5. Toss each bowl ten times and start the timer for 18 minutes.
flow.say: Bowl 1 gets no salt at all. We still toss it, so that tossing is the same for every bowl.
flow.kid: Bowl 1 gets no salt. Toss it ten times. Salt bowls 2, 3 and 4. Toss each ten times. Start the timer.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Salted Cucumber Test. Here you add a different amount of salt to each bowl.
flow.parent: Toss bowl 1 first, while the spoon is still free of salt. One of the four small heaps is left over, and it can go back in the salt jar.

flow.do: 1. Leave the bowls alone. 2. Look closely at 5, 10 and 15 minutes without stirring. 3. Draw the results table while you wait. 4. Ask what your child notices and where they think the liquid comes from.
flow.say: Look at the bottom of each bowl. What do you notice? Where do you think that liquid is coming from?
flow.kid: Do not stir. Look at 5, 10 and 15 minutes. What is at the bottom of each bowl? Draw your table.
flow.context: This is the waiting step of the Salted Cucumber Test. The slices sit with their salt for 18 minutes while you watch.
flow.parent: Only listen at this stage. Common ideas are that the salt is melting, or that the salt has turned into water. Ask how the test could tell these apart. Bowl 1 and the taste of the liquid will help.

flow.do: 1. Hold the slices of bowl 1 back with the spoon and tip the liquid into the medicine cup. 2. Read the millilitres and write the number. 3. Empty and rinse the cup, then do bowls 2, 3 and 4. 4. Bend one slice from bowl 1 and one from bowl 4.
flow.say: Read the mark at the top of the liquid. Now bend a slice from bowl 1 and a slice from bowl 4. What is different?
flow.kid: Tip the liquid from each bowl into the cup. Read the millilitres. Write them down. Bend a slice from bowls 1 and 4.
flow.context: This is the measuring step of the Salted Cucumber Test. Here you measure the liquid that collected in each bowl.
flow.parent: If a bowl holds more than the cup, measure it in two lots and add them. If bowl 4 gave less than 2 millilitres, the slices were thick or the cucumber was old. Wait 10 more minutes and measure again. Keep the slices from bowl 4 if you plan to do Bring It Back.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child claims, what they measured and why they think it happened. 2. Only then read the explanation in the parent note together. 3. Draw the bar chart and write three sentences.
flow.say: Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reason. Did water come out? Did twice the salt give twice the water? What moved it?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say what you measured. Say why you think it happened. Draw the bar chart.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Salted Cucumber Test. Here you say and write your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

ask.q: Bowl 1 was cut and tossed like the others. What does its result tell you?
good: Cutting and tossing alone bring out almost no liquid.
So the liquid in the other bowls came out because of the salt.

ask.q: Nobody squeezed the slices. So how did the water get out?
good: It moved out of the cucumber towards the salt.
The outside became saltier than the inside, and water goes to the saltier side.

ask.q: Did twice the salt give twice the liquid?
good: More salt gave more liquid, but less than double.
The first bit of salt did the most.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: a cucumber is made of cells full of watery liquid with little dissolved in it. The salt dissolved in the wet film on each cut face and made a very salty layer outside the cells. Water moved out of the cells, through their membranes, towards the saltier side. This is called osmosis. More salt usually gives more liquid, but less than double. Once the cut faces are covered in strong salt water, extra salt adds little. If your numbers do not rise from bowl to bowl, the slices were probably uneven. Say so, and try again with thinner, even slices.

check.q: Nobody squeezed the cucumber slices. What moved the water out of their cells?
options: The salt soaked it up like a sponge
Water moved towards the saltier side
The salt melted the cucumber
