check.why: The salt made the outside of the cells much saltier than the inside. Water passes through a cell membrane towards the side with more dissolved in it. Choosing 'soaked up' may mean picturing salt as a dry sponge. But the salt itself dissolved, and the water ended up as liquid in the bowl.

experiments.title: The Burrow Test: where does water last longest?
experiments.context: In this experiment you leave the same amount of water on three plates: one in the open, one in the shade and one under a cover, like a burrow. After two hours you measure what is left. You will find out how much water a desert animal saves by spending the day underground.
experiments.question: The same amount of water sits on three plates for two hours: in the sun or under a fan, in the shade, and under a cover. How much water is left on each?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Each plate starts with 30 millilitres of water. After two hours, how many millilitres will be left on the open plate, on the shaded plate and on the covered plate? Write three numbers, and write the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the place. Use three plates of the same size and put exactly 30 millilitres on each. Start and stop all three at the same time. Tilt each plate the same way when you pour the water back.

materials.item: steel plates of the same size, with a rim
a large steel bowl or a fourth plate, to cover one plate
a 10 millilitre medicine measuring cup, or a tablespoon, which holds about 15 millilitres
a sunny window sill or balcony, or a place under a ceiling fan
a phone timer, a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess. Put 30 millilitres of water on each of three plates and set them in three places. Two hours later, measure what is left and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out the water lost from each plate. Then write three sentences: what you guessed and why, what you measured, and what this means for an animal in a burrow.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: water left after 2 hours
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers depend on the weather.

setup.art: A child pouring water from a small medicine cup onto a steel plate, with two more identical plates beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Put 30 millilitres of water on each of three plates.

setup.art: Three steel plates in three places: one on a sunny balcony ledge, one on a shaded table, and one on the same table covered by an upturned steel bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Put one plate in the sun or under a fan, one in the shade, and cover the third.

setup.art: A child tilting a steel plate over a medicine cup and pushing the last drops in with a finger.
setup.caption: 3. After 2 hours, pour the water from each plate back into the cup and measure it.

flow.do: 1. Ask for three guesses, with a reason for each, and write them down. 2. Measure 30 millilitres of water onto each plate. 3. Put plate 1 in the sun or under a fan. 4. Put plate 2 in the shade, away from the fan. 5. Put plate 3 beside plate 2 and cover it with the upturned bowl.
flow.say: Each plate has 30 millilitres. How much will be left on each after two hours? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how much water each plate will keep. Say why. Put 30 millilitres on each plate. Put them in their three places.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Burrow Test. Here you guess, and you set out three plates of water.
flow.parent: Three measures of the 10 millilitre cup make 30 millilitres. So do two tablespoons. The cover should sit on the rim of the plate and close it fairly well.

flow.do: 1. After 2 hours, carry each plate carefully to the table. 2. Tilt it over the cup and push the last drops in with a clean finger. 3. Read and write the millilitres left. 4. Work out the water lost from each plate.
flow.say: Pour slowly and push the last drops in. How much is left? How much has gone?
flow.kid: Pour each plate back into the cup. Push the last drops in. Read the millilitres. Work out what was lost.
flow.context: This is the measuring step of the Burrow Test. Two hours ago you put 30 millilitres of water on each of three plates.
flow.parent: About 1 millilitre always stays stuck to a plate. It is the same for all three, so the comparison is still fair. On a damp monsoon day the differences are small. Leave the plates for 4 hours instead.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child claims, what they measured and why they think it happened. 2. Only then read the explanation in the parent note together. 3. Write three sentences in the notebook.
flow.say: Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reason. Which plate kept its water best? Why? What does that mean for a desert animal?
flow.kid: Say which plate kept the most water. Say what you measured. Say why you think it happened.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Burrow Test. Here you say and write your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

ask.q: Where did the lost water go?
good: Into the air, as water vapour.
It evaporated.

ask.q: Why did the covered plate lose so little?
good: The air under the cover soon held as much water vapour as it could.
The damp air could not get away, so no more water could leave.

ask.q: A kangaroo rat plugs her burrow with sand during the day. Why might that help?
good: The air inside stays damp and cool, so she loses less water from her skin and breath.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: water leaves a wet surface by evaporating into the air. Heat, moving air and dry air all speed this up. Under the cover, the small amount of air soon holds as much water vapour as it can, and evaporation almost stops. An animal loses water in the same way from her skin and from every breath. In a closed burrow the air is cooler and damp, so she loses far less. Above ground at noon in the Thar, she would be the plate in the sun.

check.q: Why does a small desert animal lose less water in a closed burrow?
options: The burrow has a hidden pool
The air there is cooler and damper
She stops breathing while she rests
check.why: Water evaporates slowly into cool, damp air. The air in a closed burrow is damp because the animal's own breath has added water vapour to it. Choosing 'a hidden pool' may mean thinking a desert animal must find water. Many of them survive by losing very little.

activities.title: Salty Sip: taste three waters
activities.context: In this activity you mix water that is as salty as your blood and water that is as salty as the sea, and you taste a sip of each. Then you guess whether a thirsty sailor should drink sea water.

materials.item: steel tumblers
half-litre bottles or jugs of drinking water
fine table salt and a teaspoon
a steel plate and a butter knife, for dividing a teaspoon of salt into quarters
three slips of paper marked A, B and C

activities.safety: Take only a small sip of water C and spit it out. Nobody drinks a tumbler of it.
activities.record: Write one line on how each water tasted. Then write your guess: should the sailor drink sea water, and why?

setup.art: Three half-litre bottles of water on a kitchen counter marked A, B and C, with a plate holding a level teaspoon of salt cut into four small heaps beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Leave A plain. Stir three quarters of a teaspoon of salt into B, and three teaspoons into C.

setup.art: A girl taking a small sip from a steel tumbler marked B and frowning in thought, with tumblers A and C on the table in front of her.
setup.caption: 2. Taste a small sip of each. Spit out the sip of C.

setup.art: A girl writing in a notebook with the three tumblers beside her, and a small drawing of a boat on the sea at the top of the page.
setup.caption: 3. Write how each one tasted. Then guess: should a thirsty sailor drink sea water?

flow.do: 1. Mark the three bottles A, B and C. 2. Leave A plain. 3. Level a teaspoon of salt, divide it into four parts on the plate, and stir three parts into B. 4. Stir three level teaspoons of salt into C. 5. Pour a little of each into its tumbler.
flow.say: Water A is plain. Water B has a little salt. Water C has a lot. Stir until you cannot see any salt.
flow.kid: Leave A plain. Stir a little salt into B. Stir three teaspoons into C. Pour some of each into a tumbler.
flow.context: This is the first step of Salty Sip. Here you mix three waters with different amounts of salt.
flow.parent: Water B is about as salty as blood and tears. Water C is about as salty as the sea. Do not say this yet. Keep bottle C, because Bring It Back uses it.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes a sip of A, then a small sip of B. 2. Ask what B reminds them of. 3. Your child takes a very small sip of C, spits it into the sink and rinses with A.
flow.say: Sip A. Now sip B. Have you tasted something like B before? Now a tiny sip of C, and spit it out.
flow.kid: Sip A. Sip B. What does B remind you of? Take a tiny sip of C. Spit it out and rinse.
flow.context: This is the tasting step of Salty Sip. You have three waters: plain, a little salty and very salty.

ask.q: What does water B taste like?
good: Like tears.
Like sweat on my lip.
Like thin soup with no flavour.

flow.parent: Now you can say it: B is as salty as your own blood and tears, and C is as salty as the sea. The sea is nearly four times as salty as you are.

flow.do: 1. Read the sailor question aloud. 2. Ask for a yes or a no, and a reason. 3. Your child writes the guess in the notebook. 4. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: A sailor has no drinking water left, and the sea is all around her. Should she drink it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A sailor has no fresh water. Should she drink the sea? Say yes or no. Say why. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the last step of Salty Sip. You have just tasted water as salty as the sea.
flow.parent: Most children say no because it tastes bad, or because salt makes you thirsty. Ask why salt would make a person thirsty. Leave the question open. The Salted Cucumber Test gives the reason.
flow.think: Water C is water. The sailor needs water. So what is wrong with it?

activities.title: Read a Dropping: the dark part and the white part
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at the dropping of a house gecko, a pigeon or a crow, without touching it. You will find that it has two parts, and you will work out what each part is.

materials.item: a fresh or dry dropping from a house gecko, a pigeon or a crow, left where it is
an ice-cream stick or a dry twig, to turn it over
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a notebook and pencil, and soap for washing hands afterwards

activities.safety: Do not touch any dropping with your hands. Throw the stick away afterwards, and wash your hands with soap.
activities.record: Draw the dropping at about four times its real size. Label the dark part and the white part, and write what each one is.

setup.art: A wall below a tube light with a house gecko near the light, and two small dark droppings with white tips on the floor below.
setup.caption: 1. Look for a gecko dropping below a light, or a bird dropping on a balcony ledge.

setup.art: A child crouching and using an ice-cream stick to turn over a small dark dropping with a white cap, without touching it.
setup.caption: 2. Turn it over with a stick. Find the dark part and the white part.

setup.art: A notebook page with a large pencil drawing of a dropping, the dark part labelled 'from the gut' and the white part labelled 'nitrogen waste'.
setup.caption: 3. Draw it large and label the two parts. Then wash your hands with soap.

flow.do: 1. Find a dropping. Gecko droppings lie below lights and on window sills. Bird droppings are on ledges, railings and parked scooters. 2. Look closely without touching. 3. Turn it with the stick.
flow.say: Look closely. How many colours can you see? Is one part different from the other?
flow.kid: Find a gecko or bird dropping. Do not touch it. Turn it with a stick. How many parts do you see?
flow.context: This is the first step of Read a Dropping. Here you find a gecko's or a bird's dropping and look at it closely.
flow.parent: A gecko's dropping is a dark pellet with a small white cap at one end. A bird's dropping is a white splash with a darker blob in it. If you cannot find one today, look below the tube light tomorrow morning.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child thinks each part is, and why. 2. After they answer, read the parent note together. 3. Your child draws and labels the dropping. 4. Everyone washes hands with soap.
flow.say: What do you think the dark part is? What is the white part? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what the dark part is. Guess what the white part is. Draw the dropping big. Label it. Wash your hands.
flow.context: This is the last step of Read a Dropping. You have found a dropping with a dark part and a white part.

ask.q: Your body has two separate wastes, urine and stool. Which part of the dropping matches which?
good: The dark part is like stool: it is what is left of the food.
The white part is like urine: it is waste from the animal's own cells.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: the dark part is what is left of the animal's food, and it comes from the gut. The white part is nitrogen waste from the animal's cells. It does the job that urine does for you. Birds and geckos make uric acid, which hardly dissolves, so it leaves as a paste with very little water. Both wastes leave through one opening. A grown-up human uses about a litre and a half of water a day to carry out nitrogen waste. A gecko uses a few drops.

check.q: The white cap on a gecko's dropping does the same job as which human waste?
options: Stool
Urine
Sweat
check.why: The white cap is nitrogen waste from the gecko's cells, as urea in urine is for you. Choosing 'stool' is natural, because it arrives with the dark part. But stool is what is left of food, and it never entered the body's cells.

activities.title: Bring It Back: can a limp slice become stiff again?
activities.context: In this activity you take cucumber slices that salt has made limp and put some in plain water and some in water as salty as the sea. You will see which way the water moves this time.

materials.item: limp cucumber slices from bowl 4 of the Salted Cucumber Test, or 10 fresh slices tossed with a teaspoon of salt and left for 20 minutes
steel tumblers or bowls
plain drinking water, about one tumbler
water as salty as the sea, about one tumbler: bottle C from Salty Sip, or three level teaspoons of salt stirred into half a litre of water

activities.record: Write what you guessed. After 30 minutes, write how the slices from each tumbler feel when you bend them.

setup.art: A child rinsing a handful of limp, bendy cucumber slices in a steel strainer under a kitchen tap.
setup.caption: 1. Rinse 10 limp, salted slices quickly under the tap.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers side by side, one labelled plain water and one labelled sea-strength water, each with five cucumber slices floating in it.
setup.caption: 2. Put 5 slices in plain water and 5 in water as salty as the sea.

setup.art: A child's two hands each bending a cucumber slice: the slice in the left hand stands stiff and the slice in the right hand droops over the finger.
setup.caption: 3. After 30 minutes, bend a slice from each tumbler. Which is stiffer?

flow.do: 1. Rinse 10 limp slices for a few seconds to wash off the salt. 2. Bend one, so that your child feels how limp it is. 3. Put 5 slices in plain water and 5 in the sea-strength water. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: These slices lost water to the salt. What will happen to them in plain water? And in sea-strength water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Rinse the limp slices. Put 5 in plain water. Put 5 in salty water. Guess what will happen. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bring It Back. Salt has pulled water out of these cucumber slices, and they are limp.
flow.parent: Write the guess down and do not comment on it.

flow.do: 1. After 30 minutes, take one slice from each tumbler. 2. Your child bends both and compares them. 3. Ask what they found and why they think it happened. 4. Only then read the parent note together.
flow.say: Bend one from each tumbler. Which is stiffer? Which way did the water move this time? Why?
flow.kid: Bend a slice from each tumbler. Which is stiffer? Which way did the water go this time?
flow.context: This is the last step of Bring It Back. Limp cucumber slices have sat for 30 minutes in plain water and in salty water.

ask.q: In plain water, which side had more dissolved in it: inside the cells or outside?
good: Inside the cells. So water moved in, and the slice became stiff.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: in plain water, the inside of each cell has more dissolved in it than the outside. Water moves in, the cells fill, and the slice stiffens. It will not be quite as crisp as a fresh slice. In sea-strength water the outside is still saltier than the inside, so the slices stay limp. A river fish is like the slices in plain water, with water always coming in. A sea fish is like the slices in salty water, with water always leaving. If you feel no difference, leave them for an hour.

check.q: A limp, salted cucumber slice is put in plain water. Which way does water move?
options: Into the cells
Out of the cells
It does not move
check.why: The inside of the cells now has more dissolved in it than the plain water outside. Water moves towards the side with more dissolved in it, so it goes in. Choosing 'out' may mean thinking salt always pulls water out. The direction depends on which side is saltier at that moment.

activities.title: The Cool Nose Test: catch the water in your breath
activities.context: In this activity you breathe into a cold tumbler, a tumbler at room temperature and a warm tumbler. You will see how a desert animal's cool nose takes water back from her own breath.

materials.item: dry steel tumblers of the same size
a fridge, to chill one tumbler for 20 minutes
a bowl of warm water from a geyser or a kettle, comfortable to the hand, to warm one tumbler
a dry cloth

activities.safety: Use warm water that is comfortable to touch. Do not use boiling water.
activities.record: Draw the three tumblers and shade how much mist formed inside each.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers on a table: one frosted from the fridge, one plain, and one being lifted out of a bowl of warm water and wiped dry with a cloth.
setup.caption: 1. Chill one tumbler, leave one as it is, and warm one in warm water. Dry them.

setup.art: A boy holding a steel tumbler close to his open mouth and breathing out slowly into it.
setup.caption: 2. Breathe out slowly into each tumbler five times.

setup.art: Three tumblers seen from above: the cold one covered in mist and small drops inside, the middle one with a faint mist, and the warm one clear.
setup.caption: 3. Look inside. Which tumbler caught the most water?

flow.do: 1. Take the cold tumbler from the fridge and dry it. 2. Lift the warm tumbler from the warm water and dry it well. 3. Stand all three in a row. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: You will breathe into all three. Which one will catch the most water from your breath? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Dry the cold tumbler and the warm tumbler. Stand all three in a row. Guess which will mist up most.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cool Nose Test. You have a cold tumbler, a warm tumbler and one at room temperature.
flow.parent: Put one tumbler in the fridge about 20 minutes before you begin. Work quickly once it is out, because it warms up.

flow.do: 1. Your child breathes out slowly into each tumbler five times, mouth close to the rim. 2. Look inside each one and touch the inside wall. 3. Ask what they found and why. 4. Only then read the parent note together.
flow.say: Five slow breaths into each. Now look inside and touch the wall. Where did that water come from? Why is it only on the cold one?
flow.kid: Breathe out slowly into each tumbler five times. Look inside. Touch the wall. Which one is wet?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cool Nose Test. You breathe into three tumblers at different temperatures.

ask.q: The warm tumbler stayed clear. Was there no water in those breaths?
good: The water was there as vapour, but it stayed in the air and escaped.
Only a cool surface turns the vapour back into drops.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: breath leaves the lungs warm and full of water vapour. On a cool surface the vapour turns back into liquid. On a warm surface it stays as vapour and is lost. A kangaroo rat's nose is narrow inside, and the air she breathes in cools its walls. When she breathes out, her warm breath passes over those cool walls and leaves much of its water there. Donald Jackson and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen measured this in 1964. Your own nose does a little of the same.

check.q: How does a cool nose save water for a desert animal?
options: It stops her from breathing out
Vapour in her breath turns to liquid there
It makes new water from air
check.why: Warm breath carries water vapour. When it passes over the cool walls of the nose, some vapour turns back into liquid and stays in the body. Choosing 'makes new water' mixes this up with metabolic water, which is made in the cells from food.

activities.title: Mix a Litre of ORS, and find out why it has sugar
activities.context: In this activity you mix the home recipe for ORS, the drink that replaces water and salt lost in loose motions. You taste it, and you work out why sugar is in a medicine for losing water.

materials.item: clean drinking water, exactly one litre, in a clean bottle or jug
sugar, six level teaspoons
fine table salt, half a level teaspoon
a teaspoon, a butter knife for levelling, and a clean spoon for stirring
small steel tumblers for tasting

activities.record: Write the recipe in your notebook. Under it, write one sentence on why the sugar is there.

setup.art: A one-litre steel jug of water with six level teaspoons of sugar lined up on a plate and half a teaspoon of salt beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Measure one litre of clean water, six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt.

setup.art: A girl stirring the jug with a long spoon while her younger brother watches.
setup.caption: 2. Stir until nothing is left at the bottom.

setup.art: Two children each tasting a small tumbler of the clear drink, one of them touching the corner of her eye to compare it with tears.
setup.caption: 3. Taste it. It should be no saltier than tears.

flow.do: 1. Wash hands with soap. 2. Measure exactly one litre of clean drinking water into the jug. 3. Level each teaspoon with the butter knife. 4. Add six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt. 5. Stir until all of it has dissolved.
flow.say: Level every spoon with the knife. Six of sugar and half of salt. The amounts matter, so we measure carefully.
flow.kid: Wash your hands. Measure one litre of water. Add six level teaspoons of sugar. Add half a level teaspoon of salt. Stir well.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mix a Litre of ORS. Here you measure and mix water, sugar and salt.
flow.parent: This is the home recipe that health workers teach where packets are not at hand. Too much salt is harmful, and a little too much water is not. For anyone who is ill, use a packet of ORS and ask a doctor.

flow.do: 1. Everyone tastes a little. 2. Ask why a drink for someone losing water would have salt in it, and then why sugar. 3. After your child answers, read the parent note together. 4. Drink the rest today, or throw it away after 24 hours.
flow.say: A person with loose motions is losing water. Why give salt as well? And why do you think sugar is there?
flow.kid: Taste it. Why is salt in it? Why is sugar in it? Say what you think. Then write the recipe.
flow.context: This is the last step of Mix a Litre of ORS. You have mixed one litre of water with six teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of salt.

ask.q: Your gut has no pump for water. So how does it get water into the blood?
good: It moves salt across, and water follows the salt.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: loose motions carry out salt as well as water, so both must go back. The sugar is not there for taste or for energy. The wall of the gut has a carrier that takes in sodium, from salt, only together with glucose, a sugar. Table sugar is split in the gut into glucose and another sugar. Once the sodium is inside, water follows it by osmosis. With no sugar, much less salt and water get in. With too much sugar, the extra stays in the gut and holds water there.

check.q: Why does ORS have sugar in it?
options: To make it taste nice
It helps the gut take in salt
To give the patient energy
check.why: A carrier in the gut wall takes in sodium only together with glucose. Water then follows the sodium by osmosis. Choosing 'taste' or 'energy' is sensible, but the amount of sugar is set by what the carrier needs.

activities.title: Water Accounts: your water day in beans
activities.context: In this activity you lay out beans to show all the water an adult human takes in and loses in one day. Then you try to change the account so that the person never has to drink, as a kangaroo rat does.

materials.item: dry beans, chana or rajma, or buttons
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Copy both columns into your notebook with the number of beans in each pile. Then write which piles you changed for the animal who never drinks.

setup.art: A sheet of paper divided into two columns headed Water In and Water Out, with small piles of beans in each column and a label under each pile.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two columns, Water In and Water Out. One bean stands for 100 millilitres of water.

setup.art: A child counting beans into five piles in the Water Out column, labelled urine, breath, skin, sweat and stool.
setup.caption: 2. Lay out the beans for one day. The two columns must be equal.

setup.art: A child sliding the large pile of beans labelled drinks off the paper and looking at the Water Out column with a puzzled face.
setup.caption: 3. Take away the drinks. Now change the Water Out piles until the columns match again.

flow.do: 1. Draw two columns, Water In and Water Out. 2. Under Water In, lay 15 beans for drinks, 6 for water in food and 2 for water made in the cells. 3. Under Water Out, lay 14 for urine, 4 for breath, 4 for skin and sweat, and 1 for stool. 4. Count both columns.
flow.say: Each bean is 100 millilitres, about half a tumbler. This is one day for a grown-up. Count each column. What do you notice?
flow.kid: One bean is 100 millilitres. Lay out the Water In beans. Lay out the Water Out beans. Count both columns.
flow.context: This is the first step of Water Accounts. Here you lay out beans for the water a grown-up takes in and loses in a day.

ask.q: Both columns have 23 beans. Why must they be equal?
good: If more came in than went out, the body would swell.
If more went out, the body would dry up.

flow.parent: These are rounded figures for an adult on an ordinary day. A child's numbers are smaller, and a hot day moves beans from urine to sweat. The 2 beans made in the cells are metabolic water.

flow.do: 1. Slide the 15 drink beans away. 2. Ask your child to make the columns equal again by changing only the Water Out piles. 3. For each bean they remove, ask how a real animal could do that. 4. Read the parent note together at the end.
flow.say: A kangaroo rat never drinks. Take the drinks away. Now make the two columns equal again. How could an animal really do each change?
flow.kid: Take away the drink beans. Now only 8 beans come in. Change the Water Out piles to match. Say how an animal could do it.
flow.context: This is the last step of Water Accounts. You have laid out beans for a day's water in and water out, and now the drinks are taken away.

ask.q: Only 8 beans come in now. Which Water Out pile is the biggest to cut?
good: Urine. Make it much stronger, so that it needs less water.
Then breath and skin: stay in a cool, damp burrow and have a cool nose.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer. A kangaroo rat cuts every pile. Her urine is nearly five times as strong as the strongest human urine. Her droppings are nearly dry. Her cool nose and her damp burrow cut the loss from breath and skin, and she does not sweat. She also eats dry seeds, so in real life her food pile is smaller too. A human body cannot make these cuts, which is why we must drink.

check.q: A kangaroo rat never drinks. Where does most of her water come from?
options: A store of water in her tail
Her cells make it from food
Dew that she licks at night
check.why: When cells use food for energy, hydrogen from the food joins oxygen and forms new water. A kangaroo rat makes about 54 grams of it from 100 grams of dry barley. Choosing 'a store' is the old idea about camels too, and careful measuring found no store.

projects.title: Two Eggs, Two Waters: a model of a river fish and a sea fish
projects.context: In this four-day project you dissolve the shells off two raw eggs with vinegar. That leaves each egg inside a thin skin that lets water through. Then you put one egg in plain water and one in thick sugar syrup, and measure how each changes.

materials.item: raw eggs of about the same size
white vinegar, about two cups
tall steel tumblers or glass jars
sugar, one cup, and hot water, half a cup, for the syrup
strips of paper about 1 centimetre wide and 25 centimetres long, a pencil and a ruler
a large spoon for lifting the eggs

projects.safety: Wash your hands with soap after touching raw egg, and do not eat these eggs. A grown-up makes the hot syrup and lets it cool.

schedule.what: Put each egg in a tumbler and cover it with vinegar. Watch the bubbles on the shell.
Look at the eggs. If shell is still left, pour off the vinegar and add fresh vinegar.
Rinse the eggs gently. Measure round the middle of each with a paper strip. Guess. Put one in plain water and one in cool sugar syrup.
Measure both eggs again. Say which way the water moved in each, and why. Throw the eggs away and wash up.

projects.record: Make a table with three columns: the egg, the distance round its middle on day 3, and the distance on day 4. Under it, draw each egg and add arrows to show which way the water moved.

setup.art: Two raw eggs each sitting in a steel tumbler of clear vinegar, with small bubbles covering the shells.
setup.caption: 1. Cover two raw eggs with vinegar and leave them for two days. The shells dissolve.

setup.art: A child wrapping a narrow strip of paper round the middle of a soft, shell-less, slightly see-through egg held on a large spoon, and marking the strip with a pencil.
setup.caption: 2. Measure round the middle of each soft egg with a paper strip.

setup.art: Two tumblers side by side, one labelled plain water with a large tight egg in it, and one labelled sugar syrup with a smaller, baggy egg floating in it.
setup.caption: 3. Put one egg in plain water and one in thick sugar syrup. Measure them again the next day.

flow.do: 1. Put one raw egg in each tumbler. 2. Pour in vinegar until each egg is covered. 3. Watch for two minutes. 4. Put the tumblers where nobody will knock them.
flow.say: Look at the shell. What do you see forming on it? What do you think the vinegar is doing?
flow.kid: Put an egg in each tumbler. Cover each egg with vinegar. Watch the shell. What do you see?
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Eggs, Two Waters. Here you put two raw eggs in vinegar to dissolve their shells.
flow.parent: The bubbles are carbon dioxide. Vinegar is an acid, and it dissolves the hard shell. Under the shell is a thin, tough skin, and that skin stays.
flow.wait: Leave the eggs in vinegar until tomorrow.

flow.do: 1. Look at both eggs. 2. If patches of shell are left, pour off the vinegar gently and add fresh vinegar. 3. Do not rub the eggs.
flow.say: Is any shell left? What has changed since yesterday?
flow.kid: Look at the eggs. Is any shell left? If there is, ask for fresh vinegar. Do not rub them.
flow.context: This is the second day of Two Eggs, Two Waters. Two raw eggs have been sitting in vinegar to dissolve their shells.
flow.parent: Most shells are gone in about 48 hours. Thick shells can take three days. If so, move every later step on by a day.
flow.wait: Leave the eggs in vinegar for one more day.

flow.do: 1. Stir one cup of sugar into half a cup of hot water and let it cool. 2. Lift each egg out on the spoon and rinse it gently. 3. Wrap a paper strip round the middle of each egg, mark it and measure it. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason. 5. Put egg A in plain water and egg B in the cool syrup.
flow.say: Each egg is now inside a thin skin that lets water through. What will happen to egg A in plain water? And to egg B in syrup? Why?
flow.kid: Rinse the eggs gently. Measure round each one with a paper strip. Guess what will happen. Put one in water and one in syrup.
flow.context: This is the third day of Two Eggs, Two Waters. The shells have dissolved, and each egg is held only by a thin skin.
flow.parent: Handle the eggs over a bowl, because the skin can tear. They are already a little bigger than fresh eggs, because they took in water from the vinegar. Egg B will float in the syrup. Turn it over once or twice during the day, or rest a spoon on it.

flow.do: 1. Lift out each egg, rinse it and measure round its middle again. 2. Let your child feel both gently. 3. Ask what they claim, what they measured and why. 4. Only then read the parent note together. 5. Throw the eggs away and wash hands and tumblers with soap.
flow.say: Measure both. Which grew and which shrank? Which way did the water move in each one? Why?
flow.kid: Measure both eggs again. Which grew? Which shrank? Say which way the water moved. Wash your hands.
flow.context: This is the last day of Two Eggs, Two Waters. One shell-less egg has spent a day in plain water and the other in thick sugar syrup.

ask.q: Which egg is like a river fish, and which is like a sea fish?
good: Egg A in plain water is like a river fish: water keeps coming in.
Egg B in syrup is like a sea fish: water keeps leaving.

ask.q: A real river fish does not swell up like egg A. What does she do that the egg cannot?
good: She sends the water out as lots of weak urine.
Her gills pump salt back in.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: the inside of an egg has more dissolved in it than plain water has. So water moved into egg A, and it is bigger and tight. Thick syrup has far more dissolved in it than the egg has. So water moved out of egg B, and it is smaller and baggy. Expect egg A to gain about half a centimetre to one centimetre round the middle, and egg B to lose one to two centimetres. The egg is only a model. It has no gills and no kidneys, so it shows what would happen to a fish who did nothing. If your home does not use eggs, do the same test with 20 large raisins. Put 10 in plain water and 10 in syrup for a day, then lay each ten in a line and measure the line.

check.q: A shell-less egg is put in thick sugar syrup for a day. What happens?
options: It swells, as water moves in
It shrinks, as water moves out
It stays the same size
check.why: The syrup has far more dissolved in it than the egg has. Water moves towards the side with more dissolved in it, so it leaves the egg. Choosing 'swells' may mean thinking that an egg soaks up any liquid around it. Osmosis depends on what is dissolved on each side, and sugar works just as salt does.

challenges.title: The Raita That Does Not Go Watery
challenges.context: This is a kitchen engineering challenge. In the Salted Cucumber Test, salt pulled water out of cucumber slices within minutes. That is why a cucumber raita or salad made in the morning sits in a pool of liquid by lunch.
challenges.problem: Make a salted cucumber dish that is still crisp, with almost no pool of liquid, one hour after it is packed in a lunch box.
constraints: The dish must contain cucumber and salt when it is eaten.
It must be packed at least one hour before it is eaten.
Test your design against the ordinary way: 15 slices tossed with a quarter teaspoon of salt and left for the same hour. Measure the liquid in both.
materials: two cucumbers, salt and a teaspoon
small steel boxes or bowls with lids
a knife and board, for a grown-up
optional: curd, grated coconut, soaked moong dal, roasted gram powder, a small twist of paper
general: Carry the salt separately in a twist of paper, and add it just before eating. The salt and the cells meet only at lunch.
Salt the slices first, wait 15 minutes, pour off the liquid, and then pack them. Most of the water has already left.
Cut large chunks. There are fewer cut faces for the salt to work on.
creative: Add something dry that takes up the liquid, such as grated coconut, roasted gram powder or soaked moong dal. Kosambari, the cucumber salad of Karnataka, has moong dal and coconut in it.
Scoop out the seedy middle of the cucumber, which is the wettest part, and use only the firm outer flesh.
Pack the cucumber and the salted curd in two layers that do not touch, and mix them at lunch.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Pack it and the ordinary version at the same time. After one hour, pour off and measure the liquid from each, and bend a slice from each. Write which design won, and explain it with osmosis.

setup.art: Two small steel lunch boxes side by side on a counter: one holding cucumber slices sitting in a pool of liquid, and one holding crisp slices with no pool.
setup.caption: 1. The problem: salted cucumber packed in the morning is watery by lunch.

setup.art: A child packing cucumber chunks into a steel box and placing a small twist of paper holding salt on top, beside a second box packed the ordinary way.
setup.caption: 2. Pack your design and the ordinary version at the same time.

setup.art: A child pouring liquid from a lunch box into a medicine cup while a second box waits its turn.
setup.caption: 3. After one hour, measure the liquid from each box and bend a slice from each.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and its limits aloud. 2. Ask how the water gets out of the cucumber, and what could stop it. 3. Your child chooses or invents a design and says why it should work. 4. Slice the cucumbers as the design needs.
flow.say: Salt pulls water out of cut cucumber. How could you stop that, or make it not matter? Tell me your plan and your reason.
flow.kid: Read the problem. Think: how does the water get out? Choose a plan. Say why it should work.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Raita That Does Not Go Watery. Here you plan a salted cucumber dish that will stay crisp for an hour.
flow.parent: Let your child try their own idea first, even if you can see a flaw. The test will show it.

flow.do: 1. Pack the ordinary version: 15 slices tossed with a quarter teaspoon of salt. 2. Pack your child's design in a second box. 3. Close both and note the time.
flow.say: We pack both at the same moment, so that the test is fair.
flow.kid: Pack the ordinary box: 15 slices and a quarter teaspoon of salt. Pack your design. Note the time.
flow.context: This is the packing step of the Raita That Does Not Go Watery. You pack an ordinary salted cucumber box and your own design.
flow.wait: Leave both boxes closed for 1 hour.

flow.do: 1. After one hour, pour the liquid from each box into the medicine cup and measure it. 2. Bend a slice from each and taste one from each. 3. Ask what worked and why. 4. Your child changes one thing and says what they would test next.
flow.say: How much liquid in each? Which is crisper? Is yours still salty enough to eat? What would you change?
flow.kid: Measure the liquid in each box. Bend a slice from each. Taste both. What would you change next time?
flow.context: This is the testing step of the Raita That Does Not Go Watery. Two lunch boxes of salted cucumber have been closed for one hour.
flow.parent: A design that carries the salt separately should have almost no liquid. A design salted and drained first has little new liquid, but the slices are already soft. There is a trade to weigh between crisp and ready-salted. Your child decides which matters more.

challenges.title: Design an Animal for a Place
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. You have seen how a river fish, a sea fish, a hilsa and a kangaroo rat each balance water and salt. Now you invent an animal for one place and show how her body does it.
challenges.problem: Choose one of four places. Invent an animal who can live there, and draw how she keeps her water and salt steady.
constraints: Choose one place: the dunes of the Thar, a village tank of fresh water, the open Bay of Bengal, or a mangrove creek where the water is nearly fresh at low tide and nearly sea water at high tide.
Show with arrows which way water moves across her skin or gills by osmosis.
Show how her nitrogen waste leaves: as ammonia, urea or uric acid. Say why you chose it.
Show how salt enters or leaves, and mark each place where her body must spend energy.
If she breathes with gills, water can cross them. No skin may be waterproof and breathe water at once.
materials: the 16 cards from Three Clues, if you have made them, to borrow ideas from
general: Copy the whole kit of a real animal from that place. For the village tank: hardly drink, pass a lot of weak urine, pump salt in at the gills, let ammonia wash away.
For the open sea: drink sea water, pump salt out at the gills, pass very little urine.
For the Thar: a burrow by day, strong urine, dry droppings, a cool nose and water made from food.
creative: Use the shark's way: keep enough urea in the blood to match the sea, so that water neither enters nor leaves.
Add a salt gland beside the eye or in the nose, as seabirds and sea turtles have, and let her drink the sea.
For the mangrove creek, switch between two kits with the tide as a hilsa does with the season. Or shut yourself in a damp mud burrow at low tide, as a mudskipper does.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own animal. Give her a name. Label where water goes in and out, where salt goes in and out, and what her nitrogen waste is. Then let someone ask you three hard questions about her.

setup.art: Four small labelled sketches on one sheet of paper: sand dunes, a village pond, open sea, and a mangrove creek.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one place: the Thar, a village tank, the open sea or a mangrove creek.

setup.art: A child's large pencil drawing of an invented animal with fins and a long snout, with blue arrows for water and red arrows for salt going in and out of its body.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your animal. Add arrows for water and for salt, and label her nitrogen waste.

setup.art: A girl holding up her drawing and explaining it to her mother, who is pointing at the gills and asking a question.
setup.caption: 3. Explain your animal. Someone asks three hard questions about her.

flow.do: 1. Read the four places aloud. 2. Your child chooses one. 3. Ask what the water problem of that place is, before any drawing begins.
flow.say: In that place, is water trying to get into an animal, or out of her? What about salt?
flow.kid: Choose a place. Think: does water come into an animal there, or leave her? What does salt do?
flow.context: This is the first step of Design an Animal for a Place. Here you choose a place and work out its water problem.
flow.parent: The Thar: water leaves by evaporation. The tank: water comes in and salt leaks out. The sea: water leaves and salt comes in. The creek: both, twice a day.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws the animal large. 2. They add blue arrows for water and red arrows for salt. 3. They label the nitrogen waste and mark each place that costs energy.
flow.say: Draw her big. Show me where the water goes and where the salt goes. Where does she have to spend energy?
flow.kid: Draw your animal big. Add blue arrows for water. Add red arrows for salt. Label her waste. Mark where she spends energy.
flow.context: This is the drawing step of Design an Animal for a Place. You are inventing an animal who can balance water and salt in the place you chose.
flow.parent: Remind your child of one rule only: no body pumps water. She can move salt, and water follows.

flow.do: 1. Your child explains the animal. 2. Ask three questions from the parent note. 3. Your child changes the drawing if an answer shows a gap.
flow.say: Tell me about her. Now I have three questions for you.
flow.kid: Explain your animal. Answer three hard questions. Fix your drawing if you find a gap.
flow.context: This is the last step of Design an Animal for a Place. Here you explain your invented animal and answer questions about her.
flow.parent: Three good questions. One: which side of her skin or gills has more dissolved in it, and so which way does water move? Two: she is moving water somewhere, so which salt is she moving to do it? Three: what happens to her if she is carried to one of the other three places?

worksheets.title: Osmosis, wastes and who lives where (core)

items.p: Plain water and salty water are on two sides of a cell membrane. Which way does water move?
items.why: Water moves through a membrane towards the side with more dissolved in it. This is osmosis.

items.p: The movement of water through a membrane towards the side with more dissolved in it is called ____.
a: osmosis
items.why: Osmosis needs a membrane that lets water through more easily than what is dissolved in the water.

items.p: True or false: your cells have pumps that push water across their membranes.
items.why: False. No pump for water has been found in animal cells. Cells pump salt, and water follows through water doors called aquaporins.

items.p: Match each animal to what she does with her nitrogen waste.
pairs: lets ammonia out at the gills
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A fish can wash ammonia away. A land mammal makes urea. A bird makes uric acid, which leaves as a paste. A shark keeps urea to match the sea.

items.p: Sort each living being: is water mostly coming in, or mostly leaving?
items.a: as given
items.why: Beings in fresh water are saltier than the water, so water enters them. A sea fish is less salty than the sea, and a desert animal loses water to dry air.

items.p: Why does a mackerel drink sea water all day?
opts: She loses water through her gills by osmosis
She likes the taste of salt
items.why: A bony sea fish is less salty than the sea. Water leaves her by osmosis, so she drinks to replace it and pumps the salt out at her gills.

items.p: In the Salted Cucumber Test, the bowl with no salt had almost no liquid. What does that tell you?
items.a: Cutting and tossing alone bring out almost no liquid. So the liquid in the salted bowls came out because of the salt, and not because the slices were cut.
items.why: A strong answer says what the no-salt bowl rules out. It is the bowl that the others are compared with.

items.p: Put these in order, for what happens after a very salty meal.
a: The blood becomes slightly saltier
Cells in the hypothalamus respond
The pituitary gland releases more ADH
Collecting ducts open more water doors
You pass a little dark urine
items.why: Saltier blood is detected in the brain. ADH travels to the kidneys, more water is taken back, and less leaves in the urine.

items.p: True or false: a camel carries a store of water in her hump.
items.why: False. The hump is fat. A camel lasts without drinking because she loses water slowly and can bear losing a great deal.

items.p: The white cap on a gecko's dropping is nitrogen waste made from ____ acid.
a: uric
items.why: Uric acid hardly dissolves, so it can leave the body as a paste with very little water.

items.p: Draw a fish in a pond. Add arrows to show where water enters her, where it leaves, and where salt enters.
items.a: A fish with water arrows going in at the gills, a large arrow of weak urine going out near the tail, and small salt arrows going in at the gills.
items.why: A strong drawing shows water entering without the fish drinking, a lot of urine leaving, and salt being pumped in at the gills.

items.p: A sailor drinks one litre of sea water. How much water does her body have afterwards?
items.why: Her kidneys need about one and three quarter litres of urine to send out the salt in one litre of sea water. She ends up with less.

items.p: Name three ways in which a kangaroo rat saves water.
items.a: Any three of these. Her urine is very strong. Her droppings are nearly dry. Her cool nose takes water back from her breath. She spends the day in a closed, damp burrow. She does not sweat.
items.why: Each way cuts one of the routes by which water leaves a body: urine, droppings, breath and skin.

items.p: True or false: a rehydration drink needs only water and salt.
items.why: False. The gut takes in sodium much faster together with glucose, and water follows the sodium. So the drink needs sugar too.

items.p: Draw two cells: one sitting in plain water, one in very salty water. Add arrows to show which way water moves.
items.a: The cell in plain water is large and round with arrows pointing in. The cell in very salty water is small and wrinkled with arrows pointing out.
items.why: A strong drawing shows water going into the cell in plain water and out of the cell in salty water, with the cell's size changing to match.

items.p: What is metabolic water?
opts: Water an animal stores in fat
New water that cells make from food
Water that enters through the skin
items.why: When cells use food for energy, the hydrogen in the food joins with oxygen and forms new water.

items.p: What is the job of the loop of Henle?
opts: To make the deep kidney very salty
items.why: The loop pumps salt into the deep part of the kidney. That salty zone later draws water out of the urine by osmosis.

items.p: Put these in order, for how a kidney makes strong urine.
a: The loop of Henle pumps salt into the deep kidney
The deep kidney becomes very salty
Urine runs down through it in a collecting duct
ADH opens water doors in the duct wall
Water leaves the urine by osmosis
Strong urine flows on to the bladder
items.why: The kidney cannot pump water. It builds a salty zone first, and then lets water leave the urine by osmosis.

items.p: Why can a kidney not simply pump water out of the urine?
items.a: No pump for water has been found in animal cells. Cells can pump salt. So the kidney pumps salt into the space around the tubes, and water follows by osmosis through water doors.
items.why: A strong answer names what cells can pump, which is salt, and what they cannot, which is water.

items.p: More ADH reaches the kidneys. What happens to the urine?
opts: There is more of it, and it is paler
There is less of it, and it is stronger
items.why: ADH makes the collecting ducts open more water doors. More water returns to the blood, so less urine leaves and it is stronger.

items.p: True or false: a hilsa's gills pump salt in the same direction all her life.
items.why: False. In the sea her gills pump salt out. When she enters a river, they change over and pump salt in.

items.p: Match each organ to the living being who has it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these organs does part of the work that kidneys do in a mammal: moving salt, water or waste out of the body.

items.p: The liquid from a seabird's salt glands is ____ than sea water.
a: saltier
more salty
stronger
items.why: Because the liquid is saltier than what she drank, the bird sends out the salt and keeps some of the water.

items.p: The table shows liquid from four bowls of cucumber. Did twice the salt give twice the liquid? Explain.
items.a: No. A quarter teaspoon gave 3 millilitres and a half teaspoon gave 5, which is less than double. A whole teaspoon gave 6, far less than double again. More salt gave more liquid, but each extra bit of salt added less.
items.why: A strong answer compares pairs of numbers from the table and does not stop at 'more salt, more water'.

chart.title: Made-up results from a Salted Cucumber Test

items.p: Sea water has 35 grams of salt a litre. Strong urine holds 20. How much urine removes one litre's salt?
opts: About one and three quarter litres
items.why: 35 divided by 20 is 1.75. The body must pass more water than the sea water brought in.

items.p: Sort each animal by the nitrogen waste she mainly sends out.
items.a: as given
items.why: Animals who live in water can wash ammonia away. Land mammals and frogs make urea. Birds, snakes, lizards and insects make uric acid, which needs the least water.

items.p: Draw one loop of Henle and a collecting duct inside a kidney. Shade the part of the kidney that is saltiest.
items.a: A hairpin loop dipping down from the outer kidney and coming back up, with a straight duct beside it. The shading is darkest at the bottom, around the bend of the loop.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the darkest shading at the deepest point. That is where the urine in the collecting duct loses the most water.

items.p: A shark keeps a lot of urea in her blood. Two girls disagree about what urea is.

views.who: Nandini, a girl in Class 5 (an imagined view)
views.says: Urea is waste. Every animal makes it only to get rid of nitrogen. The shark is just slow to throw hers out.

views.who: Thenmozhi, a girl in Class 5 (an imagined view)
views.says: For a shark, urea is useful. It keeps water from leaving her body. So it is not waste until she has too much.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What from this lesson supports it?
items.a: Answers vary. For Thenmozhi: the urea makes the shark as concentrated as the sea, so she does not lose water or need to drink. For Nandini: the urea still comes from breaking down protein, and the extra does leave in the end.
items.why: Both girls are using the science. The answer depends on whether 'waste' describes the substance itself or what a body does with it.

items.p: True or false: the main way desert animals survive is by storing a lot of water.
items.why: False. Careful measuring found no water store in camels or kangaroo rats. They survive by losing very little water.

items.p: A tadpole sends out ammonia. The same animal as a frog on land sends out urea. Why the change?
items.a: Ammonia is poisonous and needs a lot of water to carry it away. A tadpole lives in water, so the ammonia washes away at once. A frog on land cannot spare that much water, so the liver turns ammonia into urea, which is safer and needs far less water.
items.why: A strong answer links the waste to the amount of water the animal has around her.

items.p: In the Burrow Test, why did the covered plate lose the least water?
opts: The air under it became damp
The cover pressed the water down
items.why: The trapped air soon held as much water vapour as it could, so evaporation almost stopped. A closed burrow works the same way.

items.p: Water that cells make from food is called ____ water.
a: metabolic
items.why: Metabolic water forms when hydrogen from food joins with oxygen. A kangaroo rat lives mainly on it.

worksheets.title: Testing claims about water and salt (challenge)

items.p: A doctor claimed in 1952 that sips of sea water help a person lost at sea. What numbers would you check?
items.a: I would compare the salt in sea water, about 35 grams a litre, with the most salt that human urine can hold, about 20 grams a litre. If urine cannot be as salty as the drink, each sip costs more water than it gives. I would also ask whether he had any other water, such as rain or the liquid from fish.
items.why: A strong answer tests the claim against what kidneys can do, and asks what else could explain the man's survival.

items.p: Why does shark meat smell of ammonia when it is not fresh?
opts: Bacteria turn the urea in it into ammonia
Sea water has ammonia in it
items.why: A shark keeps a lot of urea in her blood and flesh. After death, bacteria break the urea down into ammonia.

items.p: Where did the kidney's filter first appear? Two scientists gave different answers.

views.says: In fresh water. The first animals with backbones lived in rivers, and the filter was a way to bail out the water that poured in.
In the sea. The oldest fossils of animals with backbones lie in rocks from the sea, and hagfish have filters and never leave the sea.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? What new evidence could change your mind?
items.a: Answers vary. For Robertson: the fossils and the hagfish. For Smith: a filter suits a river fish's problem very well. New evidence could be older fossils from river rocks, or signs in ancient bones of the water those animals lived in.
items.why: A strong answer picks a side, gives the evidence for it, and names something that would change the answer. This question is still argued about.

items.p: A runner drinks six litres of plain water in three hours. What happens to her blood and her cells? Why?
items.a: Her kidneys can send out only about one litre of extra water an hour, so about three litres stay. Her blood becomes too watery. Now the inside of her cells has more dissolved in it than the liquid outside, so water moves into the cells and they swell. Swollen brain cells make her confused and ill.
items.why: A strong answer uses osmosis in the other direction: when the outside is too watery, water moves into the cells.

items.p: True or false: a rehydration drink with twice the sugar works twice as well.
items.why: False. The extra sugar cannot all be taken in. It stays in the gut and holds water there by osmosis, which makes diarrhoea worse.

items.p: Which change would let a human gain water by drinking sea water?
opts: Urine that could be saltier than the sea
items.why: If urine were saltier than the drink, the salt could leave in less water than came in. Seabirds manage this with salt glands.

items.p: Put these in order, for a hilsa leaving the sea to lay her eggs.
a: In the sea she drinks and pumps salt out
She enters the brackish estuary
Over some days her gill cells change over
She stops drinking
In the river she pumps salt in and passes weak urine
items.why: In the sea, water leaves her. In the river, water enters her. Her gills and kidneys reverse their work as she passes through the estuary.

items.p: Draw a sea turtle. Show where her extra salt leaves, and where her nitrogen waste leaves.
items.a: A turtle with thick drops leaving beside her eyes, labelled salt from the salt glands, and waste leaving from the opening under her tail.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two separate routes. Salt leaves through glands beside the eyes. Nitrogen waste leaves at the other end of her body.

items.p: Textbooks say the white of a bird's dropping is uric acid. A 2019 study found none. What should scientists do next?
items.a: Test many more kinds of birds, including the ones in the older studies. Test droppings the moment they leave the bird and again some hours later, to see whether they change. Test the waste inside the bird before it reaches the gut, to see whether microbes change it.
items.why: A strong answer does not simply pick a side. It says which new measurements would settle the question.

items.p: Thick cucumber slices are salted in one bowl and thin slices in another. Why is this not a fair test of salt?
opts: Two things were changed at once
items.why: Thin slices have more cut surface for the same weight. If the bowls differ, nobody can tell whether the salt or the thickness caused it.

items.p: Water that is saltier than a river but less salty than the sea is called ____ water.
a: brackish
items.why: Brackish water is found in estuaries, backwaters and mangrove creeks, where river water and sea water mix.

items.p: Match each water problem to a way of solving it.
pairs: pass a lot of weak urine
Water keeps leaving into the sea
drink, and pump salt out at the gills
make water from food and lose very little
Sea water to drink, but weak kidneys
pump salt out through a gland
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A pond fish, a sea fish, a kangaroo rat and a seabird each face one of these problems. Each answer moves salt or cuts a loss of water.

items.p: True or false: a river fish put into sea water would swell up.
items.why: False. The sea is saltier than she is, so water would leave her and she would shrivel. She would swell only in water less salty than herself.

items.p: An animal's strongest urine holds 20 grams of salt a litre. Can she gain water from a drink with 10 grams?
items.a: Yes. One litre of the drink brings in 10 grams of salt. Her kidneys can send out 10 grams in half a litre of urine. So she keeps about half a litre of the water.
items.why: A strong answer compares the saltiness of the drink with the strongest urine. A drink weaker than the strongest urine gives a gain.

items.p: Sort each statement: is it settled, or still argued about?
items: Bony sea fish drink sea water
The kidney's filter first appeared in fresh water
A camel's hump holds no water store
The white of a bird's dropping is still uric acid when it leaves
Some salt carriers drag water through with them
A drink of salt, sugar and water can treat severe diarrhoea
items.a: as given
items.why: The settled ones have been measured many times in different ways. The others have evidence on more than one side.

items.p: A Paramecium is moved from pond water into slightly salty water. What does the contractile vacuole do?
items.why: With saltier water outside, less water enters the cell by osmosis. There is less to bail out, so the vacuole fills and empties more slowly.

quiz.p: Water passes through a cell membrane by osmosis. Which side does it move towards?
opts: The side with more dissolved in it
The side with less dissolved in it
quiz.why: Water moves towards the side with more dissolved in it. Salt, sugar and urea all have this effect.

quiz.p: A dry raisin left in a tumbler of water swells. Why?
opts: Water moves into the sugary raisin
Sugar moves out and leaves a gap
quiz.why: The inside of a raisin has a lot of sugar dissolved in very little water. Water moves in by osmosis.

quiz.p: Why does drinking sea water leave a person with less water?
opts: Removing its salt takes more water than it gives
quiz.why: Sea water is saltier than the strongest human urine. The kidneys must use more than a litre of water to send out the salt from one litre.

quiz.p: What does ADH, the water-saving hormone, tell the kidneys to do?
opts: Take more water back from the urine
quiz.why: ADH makes the collecting ducts open more water doors. More water returns to the blood, and less leaves as urine.

quiz.p: Which part of a kidney tube makes the deep kidney very salty?
quiz.why: The loop of Henle pumps salt out into the deep part of the kidney. That salty zone draws water out of the urine.

quiz.p: Which animal sends out nitrogen waste as a paste, with very little water?
quiz.why: Birds make uric acid, which hardly dissolves. It leaves as the white part of the dropping. A cow makes urea and a sardine lets out ammonia.

quiz.p: Ammonia is poisonous. Why can a pond fish still use it as her nitrogen waste?
opts: Fish are not harmed by poison
It washes away into the water at once
She stores it in her bones
quiz.why: Ammonia dissolves very easily. It passes out through her gills into the water around her before it can build up.

quiz.p: Which is true of a fish living in a river?
opts: She passes a lot of weak urine
She pumps salt out at her gills
quiz.why: Water enters a river fish by osmosis, so she sends it out as plenty of weak urine. She hardly drinks, and her gills pump salt in.

quiz.p: A sea fish is put into a bucket of tap water. What happens to her?
opts: Water moves out of her body
quiz.why: She is saltier than tap water, so water moves in by osmosis. Her gills are set to pump salt out, which now makes things worse.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT a way a kangaroo rat saves water?
opts: A store of water in her tail
quiz.why: No desert animal studied so far carries a tank of water. A kangaroo rat survives by losing very little.

quiz.p: In the Salted Cucumber Test, why did one bowl get no salt at all?
opts: To show what cutting alone does
quiz.why: The no-salt bowl is cut and tossed like the others. Whatever liquid it gives is not caused by salt, so the other bowls can be compared with it.

quiz.p: A rehydration drink is made with salt but no sugar. What goes wrong?
opts: The gut takes in less salt and water
Nothing: it works just as well
quiz.why: The carrier in the gut wall takes in sodium together with glucose. Without sugar, less sodium enters, and less water follows it.

applications: ORS, the drink of water, salt and sugar, treats the loss of water in diarrhoea. It works because the gut takes in salt together with sugar, and water follows.
The salt water dripped into a vein in hospital has 9 grams of salt in a litre. That matches the blood, so the blood cells neither swell nor shrink.
Salt keeps pickles and dried fish from rotting, and sugar does the same for jam and murabba. Both draw water out of microbes by osmosis.
A water purifier marked RO pushes water through a membrane against the direction of osmosis, using a pump. RO is short for reverse osmosis. The salts stay behind.
Large plants near Chennai make drinking water from sea water by reverse osmosis.
Limp greens and carrots left in a bowl of plain water become crisp again, because water moves back into their cells.
Fish farmers move young fish and prawns between waters of different saltiness slowly, over hours or days, so that their bodies can change over.
People who work or play for hours in the heat drink salted buttermilk or salted lime juice. Sweat carries out salt as well as water.
Urea is made in factories as a fertiliser. Plants take up its nitrogen and build it into new protein.

open_questions.q: Does any cell move water directly, without moving salt first?
open_questions.why_open: No pump for water has been found. But some scientists report that a few carriers of salt and sugar take water through with them, even against osmosis. Others think the measurements can be explained by ordinary osmosis. The argument is not over.

open_questions.q: How does the very deepest part of the kidney become so concentrated?
open_questions.why_open: The outer part of the salty zone is well understood. In the innermost part, the tube walls do not seem to pump salt in the same way. Several explanations have been offered since the 1970s, and none fits all the measurements.

open_questions.q: How does a hilsa or a salmon sense that the water is changing, and start to change her gills in time?
open_questions.why_open: Hormones that drive the change are known. How the fish first detects the saltiness of the water, and whether the change begins before she even reaches the river, is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How do tardigrades and some desert plants stay alive after losing almost all their water?
open_questions.why_open: A tardigrade is a tiny animal who can dry out completely and start moving again when wetted. Special sugars and proteins seem to protect the dry cells. Exactly how they do it is not yet understood.

open_questions.q: Can a small artificial kidney be worn on the body, or placed inside it?
open_questions.why_open: A dialysis machine is the size of a small cupboard and uses a great deal of water. Teams of engineers are testing small devices. None is yet in ordinary use.

maths.problem: Sea water has 35 grams of salt in a litre. The strongest human urine holds about 20 grams in a litre. A sailor drinks 2 litres of sea water. How much urine is needed to carry that salt out? How much water has she lost or gained?
maths.answer: She needs 3 and a half litres of urine. She has lost 1 and a half litres of water.
maths.explain: Two litres of sea water bring in 2 × 35 = 70 grams of salt. Each litre of urine carries out 20 grams. 70 ÷ 20 = 3.5 litres of urine. She drank 2 litres and passed 3.5 litres. 3.5 − 2 = 1.5 litres lost.
maths.context: In Salty Sip you tasted water as salty as the sea and guessed whether a thirsty sailor should drink it.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the salt in the drink by the salt that urine can carry turns 'sea water is bad for you' into an exact loss of water.

maths.problem: In a Salted Cucumber Test, a quarter teaspoon of salt gave 3 millilitres of liquid. If twice the salt always gave twice the liquid, how much would half a teaspoon and one teaspoon give? The real results were 5 and 8 millilitres. What does that tell you?
maths.answer: 6 millilitres and 12 millilitres. The real results were smaller, so twice the salt gives less than twice the liquid.
maths.explain: Half a teaspoon is twice a quarter, so 2 × 3 = 6. One teaspoon is four times a quarter, so 4 × 3 = 12. The real 5 is a little under 6, and the real 8 is well under 12. Each extra bit of salt pulls out less water than the bit before.
maths.context: This is about the Salted Cucumber Test, where you salted four bowls of cucumber slices and measured the liquid in each. These numbers are made up.
maths.why_maths: Working out what 'in proportion' would look like gives you something to compare the real results with.

chart.title: Made-up example: liquid from each bowl after 18 minutes

maths.problem: In Salty Sip, 3 level teaspoons of salt made half a litre of water as salty as the sea. How many teaspoons would a 10 litre bucket need? If one level teaspoon weighs about 6 grams, about how many grams is that?
maths.explain: Half a litre needs 3 teaspoons, so one litre needs 6. Ten litres need 10 × 6 = 60 teaspoons. 60 × 6 grams = 360 grams. That is more than a third of a one kilogram packet of salt in one bucket.
maths.context: In Salty Sip you mixed half a litre of water as salty as the sea, using 3 level teaspoons of salt.
maths.why_maths: Scaling a small recipe up shows how much salt the sea really holds, which a sip cannot tell you.

maths.problem: A kangaroo rat's cells make about 54 grams of water from 100 grams of dry barley. Suppose she eats 5 grams of barley in a day. How much water does she make? An adult human loses about 2300 millilitres a day. About how many times more is that?
maths.answer: She makes about 2.7 grams of water, which is about 2.7 millilitres. A human's daily loss is roughly 850 times as much.
maths.explain: 5 grams is one twentieth of 100 grams. 54 ÷ 20 = 2.7 grams. One gram of water is one millilitre. 2300 ÷ 2.7 is about 850. A whole day of her water is about half a teaspoon.
maths.context: In Water Accounts you laid out beans for a human's water day and then tried to live without drinking, as a kangaroo rat does. The 5 grams a day is a made-up round figure.
maths.why_maths: Finding a fraction of 54 shows how small an amount of water this animal lives on, and dividing shows how different that is from us.

maths.problem: In Water Accounts, 23 beans of water leave an adult in a day, and 14 of them are urine. What fraction is urine? If the drinks are taken away, only 8 beans come in. Breath, skin and stool use 9 beans. Why can no change to the urine alone balance the account?
maths.answer: 14 out of 23, which is a little more than half. Even with no urine at all, 9 beans would leave and only 8 would come in.
maths.explain: 14 ÷ 23 is about 0.61, or about 61 parts in 100. Without drinks, the beans coming in are 6 + 2 = 8. The beans leaving by breath, skin and stool are 4 + 4 + 1 = 9. 9 is more than 8 before any urine is counted. So an animal who never drinks must also cut what she loses from breath and skin.
maths.context: In Water Accounts you laid out beans for the water an adult takes in and loses in one day. Each bean stood for 100 millilitres.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two columns shows which losses must be cut. It explains why a burrow and a cool nose matter as much as strong urine.

maths.problem: Home ORS uses 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt in 1 litre of water. How much of each would one 250 millilitre tumbler need? Why is it better to mix a whole litre?
maths.answer: One and a half teaspoons of sugar and one eighth of a teaspoon of salt. One eighth of a teaspoon is too small to measure well.
maths.explain: 250 millilitres is a quarter of a litre. A quarter of 6 is 1.5. A quarter of a half is one eighth. A small mistake with one eighth of a teaspoon could double the salt, and too much salt is harmful. In a whole litre, half a teaspoon can be levelled properly.
maths.context: In Mix a Litre of ORS you measured six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt into one litre of water.
maths.why_maths: Scaling the recipe down shows when an amount becomes too small to measure safely.

warmup.q: Which way does water move through a cell membrane?
warmup.a: Towards the side with more dissolved in it. This is called osmosis.

warmup.q: Why can a thirsty sailor not drink sea water?
warmup.a: Sea water holds more salt than the strongest human urine can. Sending the salt out takes more water than the sea water gave.

warmup.q: Does a river fish drink a lot or hardly at all?
warmup.a: Hardly at all. Water is already entering her through her gills by osmosis.

warmup.q: What is the white part of a gecko's or a bird's dropping?
warmup.a: Nitrogen waste made from uric acid. It does the job that urine does for us, with very little water.

warmup.q: What is in a camel's hump?
warmup.a: Fat. It is a store of food, and it holds no store of water.

warmup.q: What does the water-saving hormone, ADH, do?
warmup.a: It tells the kidneys to take more water back from the urine. The urine becomes less and stronger.

warmup.q: Where does a kangaroo rat get her water?
warmup.a: Her cells make it from her food. It is called metabolic water.

warmup.q: Why does ORS have sugar in it as well as salt?
warmup.a: The gut takes in salt much faster together with sugar. Water then follows the salt.

roots.context: We have learned how bodies keep their water and salt steady in rivers, seas and deserts. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Salted Cucumber Test, nobody squeezed the slices. You put salt outside them, and water came out. Kidneys, fish gills and a seabird's salt glands all work in this way. They spend energy on moving salt, and the water follows without being pushed. So an animal steers her water by moving something else.
deep_truth.habit: We assume that to move a thing, you must push that thing. So we picture the kidneys pumping water, as a motor pumps water up to a tank. No pump for water has been found in any animal cell. Life sets up a difference in salt, and water does the rest.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Salted Cucumber Test, salt on the outside brought water out of the cells, and the bowl with no salt stayed almost dry. In Bring It Back, plain water outside sent the water in again. A kidney tube pumps salt out so that water returns to the blood. A sea fish's gut pumps salt in so that the sea water she drank follows it.

three.who_am_i: You are mostly water, and you have never pushed a drop of it. Your cells move salt, and your water goes where the salt has gone.
three.what_is_life: Every living being, from a Paramecium to a camel, keeps an inside that is different from the outside. Each one senses their own water and acts on it. Staying alive means keeping that difference going, every second.
three.what_is_this_world: The same water is too much for a river fish, too little for a sea fish and deadly for a sailor to drink. What water is to a body depends on the body it meets.

roots.thread: Water alone, with nothing in it, has no direction to go. Put a membrane in it, and a little more salt on one side than the other, and the water begins to move. One small difference is enough to start a flow. Living bodies are made of such differences, kept up by cells that never stop moving salt. The sea fish, the river fish, the gecko and you are many ways of holding the same kind of difference. A Paramecium senses the water coming in and bails it out. A hilsa senses the river and changes her gills. Each being decides, in their own way, what to do about their water. When the difference is gone, the flow stops, and the body is no longer separate from the water around it.

science.text: Water crosses cell membranes through aquaporins, which are doors and not pumps. The direction is set by osmosis.
Some scientists report that a few carriers of salt and sugar take water through with them, even against osmosis. Others explain the same results by ordinary osmosis.

other_view.view: Water is not following anything, and a body is not steering anything. Water particles move at random in all directions. Where more is dissolved, slightly fewer of them cross, and the numbers do the rest. Words such as 'steer', 'follow' and 'decide' are our way of telling the story. On this view a kidney is a mechanism shaped by natural selection, and nothing in it chooses.

practice.title: Hold a sip, and notice where the water goes
practice.say: Sit comfortably with a tumbler of plain water. Take one small sip and hold it in your mouth. Do not swallow yet. Breathe slowly ten times through your nose. The cells of your cheeks and tongue are saltier than this water. Some of the water is already moving into them. Now swallow. Sit for ten more slow breaths. Within a few minutes some of that sip will be in your blood. Your gut is moving salt, and the water is following it. You are not doing anything, and it is happening.
practice.kid: Take a small sip of water. Hold it in your mouth. Breathe slowly ten times. Your mouth is saltier than the water. Some water is already going into your cells. Now swallow. Breathe ten more times. Nobody is pushing that water. It is following the salt.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge in this lesson was reasoned through step by step as a family in a city flat would do it. None has yet been tried at home, so please treat times and amounts as a starting point. The Salted Cucumber Test (in the core path) needs two firm cucumbers, salt, four small bowls and a 10 millilitre medicine cup. Slices as thick as a 5 rupee coin, and even, matter most. Expect a few drops from the bowl with no salt and roughly 5 to 10 millilitres from the bowl with one teaspoon, but cucumbers vary a lot. If bowl 4 gives under 2 millilitres, wait 10 more minutes. In Salty Sip, the sea-strength water is only sipped and spat out. In Bring It Back, the slices in plain water become stiffer within about 30 minutes but not as crisp as fresh ones. If they do not, leave them for an hour. The Burrow Test depends on the weather: on a damp monsoon day leave the plates for 4 hours. In Read a Dropping, nobody touches the dropping, and hands are washed with soap. The Cool Nose Test needs one tumbler chilled for 20 minutes beforehand. Mix a Litre of ORS is for learning. Anyone who is ill should have a packet of ORS and see a doctor. Two Eggs, Two Waters takes four days, and thick shells can need a third day in vinegar. The eggs are not eaten. Homes that do not use eggs can do the raisin version given in the last step. Cross the Thar was checked by playing it 20,000 times on a computer for each pair of tricks. With 7 beans and no useful tricks an animal crosses about one time in four. With Burrow by Day and Warm-Up Body it crosses about four times in five. Three Clues was read through for two players and for one player alone. Facts checked against published sources while writing: the range of human urine strength and the strength of blood plasma, the salt in sea water and in the strongest urine, the kangaroo rat study of 1948 and its figure of 54 grams of water from 100 grams of barley, the strongest urine of beaver, human and kangaroo rat, the camel's body temperature swing and the water loss she can bear, the nose study of 1964, the nitrogen wastes of fish, mammals, birds and reptiles, the hilsa's rivers and season, the 1953 and 1971 ORS studies and their figures, the home ORS recipe, and the 2019 study of bird droppings.
